Article Title: How Intel Core Ultra processors lead in performance where Qualcomm ‘struggles’
Article Text:
Software and enterprise compatibility

Performance in real-world workloads and gaming

Meanwhile, Snapdragon uses ARM architecture to maximise battery life and efficiency at the expense of gaming performance.

Moreover, Snapdragon delivers Copilot+ AI experiences – the major difference is that Intel brings those AI experiences to the full Windows ecosystem – with native compatibility for the applications, peripherals, management tools, and developer workflows that businesses and creators already rely on.

Intel-exclusive technologies

The Times of India has reached out to Qualcomm for a comment.

We grew up with “Intel Inside” stickers on our PCs, a branding that made an invisible component a household symbol of trust and raw performance. Yet recent years brought turbulence, with rivals like Qualcomm squeezing Intel’s core market. Today, under the leadership of Lip-Bu Tan, the turnaround seems real. Backed by Washington and crucial partnerships with titans like Nvidia, Intel is regaining its operational stride. The legacy chipmaker launched the Core Ultra Series 3 processors (codenamed Panther Lake) at this year’s CES as Intel's first mobile platform built on the advanced Intel 18A process node – its biggest process innovation – making a strong case for its Core Ultra Series 3 processors in the AI PC race.Given the data in the public domain, the company’s chips hold a clear advantage over its competitors like Qualcomm’s Snapdragon platform – which compete in the same domain – in three areas: software and enterprise compatibility, real-world workloads like gaming and technologies that only Intel offers. Here is what Intel offers.Intel Core Ultra Series 3 processors are built on the x86 architecture. This essentially means the full Windows and Chrome OS software ecosystem runs natively on them, with no emulation and no workarounds.For businesses, Intel says this brings native compatibility with decades-old business applications or software, established security agents and enterprise management tools. It also covers the range of peripheral devices that organisations already use.Intel vPro adds another layer on top. According to the company, it gives IT teams a hardware-based way to remotely manage, secure and support devices across large fleets. This includes out-of-band management that works independently of the operating system. Intel describes it as a capability built and tested over years of enterprise use, and one of its strongest selling points for corporate PC buyers.Intel also points to its AI PC platform, which it says supports more than 500 optimised AI models. The company says over 100 independent software vendors (ISVs) are engaged in optimising software for AI PCs.On the performance side, Intel says Core Ultra Series 3 delivers up to 180 TOPS of total AI compute. This comes from the CPU, GPU and NPU working together. The company explains that this mixed design sends each AI workload to the most efficient processing engine for the job, instead of depending on one type of processor. In practice, Intel says this keeps performance steady when several tasks run at once, such as content creation, AI inferencing, video calls and background processes.Gaming is another area Intel highlights. Its x86 architecture works with the full Windows gaming ecosystem. That includes anti-cheat software, older titles, specialised controllers and peripheral drivers. Intel says these are areas where mobile-first architectures still face compatibility gaps.Intel also has a few technologies that set its platform apart.Integration of these standards delivers up to 120 Gbps of bandwidth. It supports fast data transfer, daisy-chained displays and universal docking. Intel says this is supported natively across its platforms but is not available on mobile-first architectures.This enables hardware-accelerated video encoding and decoding directly on the processor. Intel says content creators working with high-resolution footage get faster export times, without the CPU load that software encoding demands.
Article Summary: Intel Core Ultra Series 3 processors are built on the x86 architecture. This essentially means the full Windows and Chrome OS software ecosystem runs natively on them, with no emulation and no workarounds. For businesses, Intel says this brings native compatibility with decades-old business applications or software. Intel also points to its AI PC platform, which it says supports more than 500 optimised AI models.

Article Title: Jamie Dimon, longest-serving CEO of America's biggest bank, has a 'huge worry' and as an answer to US-China's ‘big problems’
Article Text:
Jamie Dimon: My biggest concern is geopolitics, world peace

Growth as the antidote to US-China tension

A consistent voice on geopolitical risk

A closely watched Wall Street voice

Jamie Dimon the longest-serving CEO of America's largest bank, JPMorgan Chase recently said that his ‘huge worry’ is that slowing economic growth could make it harder to address major challenges facing both the United States ans China, arguing that stronger growth remains the best solution to many global problems, according to a report by South China Morning Post. Speaking about geopolitical and economic tensions, Dimon said growth is a powerful force that can help countries navigate difficult issues ranging from trade disputes and debt burdens to broader international rivalries.Speaking to the South China Morning Post during a recent visit to Hong Kong, Dimon was direct about what keeps him up at night, saying his biggest worry isn't tied to markets or interest rates, but to the broader state of global peace. The comment came during a trip packed with meetings involving entrepreneurs and business leaders connecting China to global markets, just days before Dimon boarded a private plane back to Washington for a state dinner at the White House welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping.Despite flagging world peace as his top concern, Dimon struck a relatively upbeat tone on the current moment, saying there's reason for some genuine optimism given how things stand today.The Hong Kong visit of Dimon came in the same stretch as a round of trade talks hosted at JPMorgan Chase's New York headquarters, involving Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng alongside senior US officials including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. Against that backdrop, Dimon expressed pride in what he described as a vibrant, healthy, and innovative US economy, while also acknowledging some of the country's own shortcomings.His broader message centered on the idea that sustained economic growth, rather than confrontation, offers the most realistic path toward easing tension between the world's two largest economies — a theme he's returned to repeatedly over the years as he's weighed in on the US-China relationship.This isn't the first time Dimon has flagged geopolitical instability as the defining risk of the moment. He has repeatedly argued in recent years that geopolitical tensions, rather than traditional economic indicators, pose the single biggest threat to the global economy — at one point describing an "evil axis" of adversarial nations as his top concern for the next century, and separately urging Americans to stop viewing China as an unbeatable "10-foot giant," even as he's cautioned that the US needs to "take a deep breath" and restructure trade policy around national security considerations.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan Chase for more than two decades, is among the most influential voices in global finance. His views are closely monitored by investors, policymakers and business leaders because of the bank's position as the largest lender in the US by assets.In recent years, he has repeatedly called for pragmatic engagement between major economies while warning about the risks posed by geopolitical instability, rising debt levels and structural economic weaknesses.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon says slowing economic growth could make it harder to address major challenges facing the United States and China. Dimon said growth is a powerful force that can help countries navigate difficult issues ranging from trade disputes and debt burdens to broader international rivalries.

Article Title: Facebook tests Reels-style full-screen video as it prepares new apps for sellers and creators
Article Text:
Facebook tests Reels-style full-screen video as it prepares new apps for sellers and creators

Facebook tests a video-first experience

Facebook launches Seller app for frequent sellers

Meta-owned Facebook is testing a new full-screen video experience that could change what users see when they open the app. The company said it will begin testing the video-first experience later this year, putting some users directly into full-screen video instead of the usual Feed. The move comes as Facebook marks 10 years of Marketplace and launches new tools for sellers, including a separate app called Seller. In a note by Tom Allison, Head of Facebook, Meta, the company said that it is also rolling out a free verification badge and bringing more AI tools to people who sell, create and build communities on the platform.Tom Alison said the company is working on a new experience for people who want more video on Facebook. “Beyond evolving the tools for people who do things on Facebook, we’re also thinking about the experience for people who come to be entertained and connect with authentic creators. People are showing us they want more immersive, visual, video-forward experiences, and video is where conversations are happening, communities are forming, and even commerce is starting to take place,” Alison said.“So later this year, we’ll begin testing a reimagined experience that puts a subset of people who we think want more video on Facebook into full-screen video the moment they open the app,” he added.Under the test, some users will see full-screen video as soon as they open the Facebook app. The company's Classic Feed will remain available as a second tab.The video test is being announced as Facebook Marketplace reaches its 10th anniversary.Alison said Marketplace was created after Facebook noticed people were already using Groups to buy and sell products.Facebook is also testing a new app called Seller, designed for people who sell frequently on Marketplace. The app brings several selling tools together in one place. These include:- AI-powered listing creation- A unified inbox- Inventory management- Performance insightsThe app will remain connected to Facebook, meaning sellers can continue reaching buyers and their communities through the same network. Facebook said the goal is to make selling easier for people who list large numbers of products.
Article Summary: Facebook tests Reels-style full-screen video as it prepares new apps for sellers and creators. The move comes as Facebook marks 10 years of Marketplace and launches new tools for sellers, including a separate app called Seller. The company's Classic Feed will remain available as a second tab.

Article Title: Anthropic launches a 12-week 'residency' for AI engineers, modelled on how doctors train; company says: Those who pass earn the...
Article Text:
Anthropic's $100 million bet on AI talent

Anthropic's AI residency starts with a simulated deployment and a graded exam

Only nominated engineers get a seat at Claude Frontier Academy

Anthropic has launched Claude Frontier Academy, a $100 million programme that trains AI engineers the way hospitals train doctors. At its centre is a 12-week residency, where engineers lead a real Claude project at their own company under the watch of Anthropic's team before they are certified.The company plans to put 10,000 Frontier Deployed Engineers (FDEs) through the programme by the end of 2027. Its first cohorts include engineers from Accenture, Bain, Capgemini, Deloitte, McKinsey, Morgan Stanley, Novo Nordisk and Commonwealth Bank of Australia. Anthropic says people who can take AI from an idea to a working system inside a business have become the hardest talent to find, and it would rather build them than wait for the market to supply them.The comparison to medicine is deliberate. Doctors learn from practising physicians, train on real cases and are assessed before they work alone. Anthropic has built its programme on the same three steps.It starts with a multi-day, in-person session led by Anthropic engineers and licensed instructors. Participants work through a simulated enterprise deployment, from picking the right use case to security review and handover.A graded practical on a new scenario closes this stage, and those who clear it earn the Claude Resident Engineer badge.The residency comes next. Over 12 weeks, each engineer leads a real Claude use case back at their organisation, supported by Anthropic engineers and learning alongside their cohort. A final assessment decides who earns the Claude Frontier Deployed Engineer badge. The first are expected in early 2027.Seats aren't open to all. Companies nominate their strongest hands-on software engineers, and each arrives with a named Claude project to lead. Anthropic is looking for a record of building with large language models and helping others adopt AI. Prior experience building AI agents, though, isn't required. Cohorts are currently running in San Francisco, New York and London."Claude Frontier Academy trains people the way our own engineers learn," said Steve Corfield, Anthropic's global head of business development and partnerships.The FDE title is a twist on forward-deployed engineers, a role Palantir popularised by placing engineers inside client organisations. Draup data shows FDE openings at five major consulting firms rose to 1,404 in the year ended May, even as overall job postings across seven firms fell about 24%.The Academy builds on the Claude Partner Network, where professionals at 46,000 firms already hold more than 175,000 Claude certifications. Anthropic calls the 10,000-engineer target the first step of many.
Article Summary: Anthropic launches Claude Frontier Academy to train AI engineers. The company plans to put 10,000 Frontier Deployed Engineers through the programme by the end of 2027. The first cohorts include engineers from Accenture, Bain, Capgemini, Deloitte, McKinsey and Novo Nordisk.

Article Title: CurvetAI raises Rs 6 crore in funding led by Merak Ventures
Article Text: AI workspace startup CurvetAI has raised Rs 6 crore in a pre-seed funding round led by Merak Ventures, with participation from angel investors. The company will use the money to strengthen its technology infrastructure, hire staff and develop capabilities that allow AI agents to execute workflows for users.Founded in December 2025 by Vivek Dubey and Utkarsh Gupta, the Pune-based company provides access to multiple AI models through a single platform. Users can compare outputs and combine text, image, audio and video capabilities within a project.CurvetAI said it has more than 1 lakh monthly users worldwide, with India and the United States its largest markets. It has begun generating revenue but did not disclose revenue figures, the number of paying customers or its valuation following the funding round.“The user is still expected to understand which model is best for a particular task and then figure out how to make different tools work together. We believe that complexity should sit with the platform,” said Dubey, co-founder and CEO.The company initially offered a platform for discovering AI tools and prompts. It subsequently shifted towards a workspace where users could access and combine models without moving between separate products.CurvetAI said its platform is used by individuals, teams and educational institutions. It has collaborations with GnaniAI, Rumik AI and Alibaba, although the announcement did not detail their commercial terms.“What gave us conviction was the founders’ ability to translate that insight into a product people were already using at scale, and to keep evolving it as the market moved,” said Sheetal Bahl, founding partner at Merak Ventures.The company also provides a distribution channel for model developers to reach users and collect feedback. Its planned agent-based capabilities are intended to handle more complex tasks on behalf of users.
Article Summary: CurvetAI has raised Rs 6 crore in a pre-seed funding round led by Merak Ventures, with participation from angel investors. The company will use the money to strengthen its technology infrastructure, hire staff and develop capabilities that allow AI agents to execute workflows for users.

Article Title: UIDAI announces new SOP for changing name on Aadhaar, here's what you need to know
Article Text:
UIDAI announces new SOP for changing name on Aadhaar, here's what you need to know

The basic rules for name change in Aadhaar

What counts as a minor Aadhaar name change

Expanding or abbreviating initials (for example, T R D Prasad becoming Tadi Rama Durga Prasad)

Adding or deleting a middle or last name

Changing the sequence or order of an existing name (Divakar Anand to Anand Divakar)

Minor spelling corrections (Ram to Rama)

Regional language errors get their own track

Marriage or divorce-related surname changes require an affidavit (Annexure D) along with PoI.

Name changes due to gender transition require applicable PoI documentation.

Updating a child's Aadhaar from "Baby of ___" to an actual name can be done on a Head-of-Family basis, with applicable PoR.

Dropping ranks, designations, or prefixes, and removing random capital letters or dots, require no supporting documents at all.

Removing an "urf" or alias entry requires an affidavit along with PoI or PoR.

Major name changes need a Gazette Notification

How many times can you change your name on Aadhaar card

What users need to do to for name change on Aadhaar card

Visit an Aadhaar Seva Kendra or Aadhaar Enrolment/Update Centre. the process requires an in-person visit; it is not currently available end-to-end online for most categories of name change.

Fill out the Aadhaar Enrolment/Update form, writing the name in block letters, free of titles, aliases, or unapproved abbreviations.

Submit the prescribed supporting documents based on the specific category the request falls under — ranging from a simple PoI for minor corrections to a mandatory Gazette Notification for a major name change.

Complete identity verification and biometric authentication at the centre as part of the same visit.

Pay the applicable demographic update fee, currently listed by UIDAI at ₹75 when a name update is processed as a standalone request.

Collect the acknowledgement receipt, which includes an Update Request Number (URN) that can be used to track the status of the request online afterward.

UIDAI (Unique Identification Authority of India) has issued a revised Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for updating names in Aadhaar. The authority has introduced separate rules and documents requirements depending on the type of name change being requested. The new SOP, which came into effect on September 18, 2026, replaces the earlier process introduced in 2021. The updated procedure categorises requests into multiple categories, including minor spelling corrections, data-entry errors, surname changes after marriage or divorce, regional-language corrections and major name changes. According to UIDAI, documents, affidavits and Gazette notifications submitted with requests will be subject to stricter verification to prevent misuse and identity-related fraud.Under the revised SOP, names recorded in Aadhaar must appear in block letters, with no titles, prefixes (such as Shri, Smt, Ms, Dr, or Prof), aliases, ranks, or special characters permitted. Updates are governed under Regulation 19 of the Aadhaar (Enrolment & Update) Regulations, 2016, and any name change must be backed by documents listed under Schedule II. A name will be updated exactly as it appears — in spelling, sequence, and abbreviation — in the document the applicant submits as proof.UIDAI treats several routine corrections as minor name changes, requiring only standard Proof of Identity (PoI), or Proof of Relationship (PoR) for children under 18:These are accepted as long as the new name matches a PoI or PoR document the applicant has already submitted to UIDAI in the past.A separate category covers cases where the English spelling of a name on Aadhaar is correct, but the regional-language version contains an error — for instance, निर्मला being incorrectly recorded as निर्मल. These cases also require a standard PoI document to correct.Special cases with dedicated requirementsThe SOP carves out specific documentation paths for several commonly occurring situations:The strictest category under the new SOP covers a complete change of name or identity — for example, Ram Gupta becoming Shyam Gupta, or a more substantial identity shift. For these cases, UIDAI will accept only a Gazette Notification as proof, alongside standard identity documents; no other form of documentation is considered sufficient. The authority will also cross-check the proposed new name against every name previously recorded for that Aadhaar holder, and verify the authenticity of the Gazette Notification and any affidavits submitted.Under UIDAI's existing framework, a person can generally update their Aadhaar name twice in total. Once that limit is exhausted, any further name change requests must go through a separate exception-handling process. For context, gender on Aadhaar can typically be changed only once, and date of birth only once as well, under separate SOPs UIDAI maintains for those fields.To apply for a name correction or change under the new SOP, applicants need to follow a set sequence of steps:
Article Summary: UIDAI has issued a revised Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for updating names in Aadhaar. The new SOP, which came into effect on September 18, 2026, replaces the earlier process introduced in 2021. The updated procedure categorises requests into multiple categories, including minor spelling corrections, data- entry errors and surname changes after marriage or divorce.

Article Title: As Google and SpaceX plan to solve the 'data centers problem' by taking them to the Sun; some researchers in Japan and Germany want to fix it right on Earth, and their solution is ...
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representation

How elastocaloric cooling works

How elastocaloric cooling can help data centers

Technology is still at the proof-of-concept stage

Data centers are putting increasing pressure on power grids as demand for computing continues to grow. Some companies are exploring alternatives such as solar-powered facilities while tech giants like Google and SpaceX are even planning to move data centers away from Earth. Recently, Google launched its homegrown AI chips into orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of Project Suncatcher, its effort to develop solar-powered AI computing infrastructure in space. The launch marked the project's first in-orbit test, which aims to use continuously available solar power and the “infinite real estate” of orbit for AI computing.As this approach explores moving computing infrastructure off-planet, researchers in Japan and Germany are working on a way to tackle the data center cooling problem without leaving Earth. Their solution uses shape memory alloy films in a system called “elastocaloric cooling.” The technology, known as “elastocaloric cooling,” uses a titanium-nickel alloy film that changes shape in response to heat and drives a refrigeration cycle. The study, published in Nature Energy, presents a prototype that could eventually find applications in data centers and other computing devices, although the current system remains at the proof-of-concept stage.The prototype consists of a thermal actuator and a cooling unit. Its thermal actuator uses a shape memory alloy film made from titanium-nickel. When the film reaches a sufficiently high temperature, it stretches and generates force that elongates a separate refrigerant film.The refrigerant film eventually contacts a heat sink, which removes heat from the film. As the actuator and refrigerant films cool, they return to their original shapes. The refrigerant film then contacts the heat source and absorbs heat, restarting the cycle.According to the researchers, the cooling process takes place through four steps involving the heating, deformation, cooling and recovery of the films. The system is designed to repeat the process continuously without requiring a conventional motor to drive the cooling operation.The research paper does not specifically propose the technology for data center cooling. However, the approach could potentially address one of the challenges associated with large computing facilities: the energy and water required to keep hardware within operating temperatures.Data centers use substantial amounts of electricity, while conventional cooling systems can add to their energy requirements. Some cooling systems also use water. A cooling technology based on shape memory alloy films could potentially reduce the need for some conventional cooling infrastructure if it can be scaled.The same principle could also have applications beyond large data centers, including personal computers and other electronic devices.The prototype currently has significant limitations. The researchers reported that the films generated only **2.09 milliwatts of cooling power**. The system was also limited by relatively slow actuation and the size of its heat exchanger.These limitations mean the technology is not yet ready to replace the cooling systems used in large computing facilities. Scaling cooling output while improving the system's speed and efficiency would be necessary before practical applications become possible.Still, the research demonstrates that elastocaloric cooling can work using shape-changing films rather than conventional motor-driven refrigeration. If researchers can overcome the current limitations, the approach could eventually offer another way to manage heat in computing hardware, including the increasingly power-hungry systems used in AI data centers.
Article Summary: Researchers in Japan and Germany are working on a way to tackle the data center cooling problem without leaving Earth. Their solution uses shape memory alloy films in a system called “elastocaloric cooling.” The technology, known as ‘elast vocaloric cooling,’ uses a titanium-nickel alloy film that changes shape in response to heat. The study presents a prototype that could eventually find applications in data centers.

Article Title: India’s First Agentic AI Campus Takes Shape at KLH Hyderabad
Article Text: KLH Hyderabad today inaugurated its Agentic AI Campus initiative and signed an MoU with HCL Group AI Labs, unveiling a roadmap that places AI-powered learning and student innovation at the centre of its academic vision. The collaboration aims to equip students across disciplines to understand, build and apply intelligent technologies through practical projects, faculty mentorship and industry engagement. Mr. Deepak Sarvanan, National Head, HCL Group AI Labs, formally inaugurated the initiative at a press meet in KLH Bachupally campus in Hyderabad.Dr. L. Koteswara Rao, Principal, KLH Bachupally, represented KLH at the MoU exchange, alongside Dr. A. Srinath, Dean – Skill Development, in the presence of other senior officials, deans, faculty and staff.The initiative aims to make AI an integral part of the student experience. From exploring concepts in the classroom to developing applications, students will be encouraged to use AI to investigate problems, test ideas and create solutions relevant to industry and society.Er. Koneru Lakshman Havish, Vice President, KL Deemed to be University said, “We want students to develop the confidence and skills to shape how AI is used in their chosen fields.Our collaboration with HCL Group AI Labs will help connect classroom learning with hands-on projects and industry expertise, giving students opportunities to build intelligent solutions for real-world needs. As we develop our Agentic AI Campus, our focus is on preparing young people to innovate responsibly and contribute meaningfully to an evolving workplace. ”Agentic AI brings a new dimension to this approach. These systems can plan and carry out a series of tasks towards a defined goal, with appropriate human oversight. Understanding how such systems work will help students explore applications that extend from analysing information to coordinating workflows and supporting decisions.The proposed roadmap envisages project-based learning in areas such as business automation, data-driven services and discipline-specific AI applications. Students will be encouraged to design and test solutions, evaluating their accuracy, reliability and practical value.Faculty readiness will be a key part of the campus’s development. The collaboration envisages supporting educators in integrating AI into teaching, assignments and mentorship, helping students connect technical understanding with critical thinking and independent judgement.Responsible AI use will remain central to the learning approach, with attention to data privacy, bias, reliability and human accountability. Students will be encouraged to question outputs, verify information and understand the limitations of the systems they develop and use.Through its collaboration with HCL Group AI Labs, KLH Hyderabad aims to strengthen the connection between academic learning and the evolving workplace across its Bachupally and Aziznagar campuses, preparing students to develop AI solutions and apply them thoughtfully to real-world challenges.
Article Summary: KLH Hyderabad has signed an MoU with HCL Group AI Labs. The initiative aims to make AI an integral part of the student experience. Students will be encouraged to use AI to investigate problems, test ideas and create solutions relevant to industry and society.

US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has announced that it will soon mandate online filing for many immigration forms that have been available for e-filing for at least 180 days. The immigration authority shared a post on X (formerly Twitter), stating that “Digital submissions help us receive, store, and access information more efficiently, supporting stronger fraud detection, identity management, and national security screening.” The post also has a link to the ‘Online Filing Options’ website listing forms that are available for online filing, benefits of filing a form online, among others.There are two options for submitting forms from a USCIS online account, the webpage states. The first is filling out an online form electronically where you are guided step-by-step through the form to answer questions that are relevant to your form type and category. The second online filing option allows you to upload and submit a completed PDF file of your form and related evidence. Both filing options have similar features to manage your case in your online account.Almost all USCIS forms can be filed online. Some of these are:Sign in to your USCIS online account or create a USCIS online account, if you do not already have one. Go to our Sign Up page. If you need help creating a USCIS online account, please visit our How to Create a USCIS Online Account page.You must provide a valid email address and password to create a USCIS online account. The email address you provide will also be the username for your USCIS online account. The USCIS online account uses a two-factor authentication process. This means that in addition to entering your username and password, you must also enter a 1-time verification code that USCIS will send you by email, text message, or authentication app, each time you sign into your account. When you create your USCIS online account, you can select how you want to receive the 1-time verification code. If you select text message, enter your U.S. mobile phone number in the Mobile Number box (standard SMS/text messaging rates may apply). If you select the app option, the system will generate a code that you can scan or type into an authentication app that you have installed on your mobile device (such as Google Authenticator).To sign in to your USCIS online account using two-factor authentication:Select “File a Form Online.”Select the form you want to file.Select “Fill Out Form Fields Online.”Complete all sections of your form.Fill out all sections of the form as completely as possible.Read the form instructions for information on completing fields when your answer is “zero” or “not applicable (N/A).”Upload evidence.You may need to provide evidence when you file to support your application, petition, or request. These documents help us evaluate your form and verify information you have provided.Use these tips when uploading evidence:If USCIS require passport-style photos, you must either scan them or take a picture with your phone.Review and digitally sign your form.Review the summary of the information you provided in your application, petition, or request. You may save and print a copy for your records.To digitally sign your application, petition, or request, enter your full legal name (first, middle, and last names) in the space provided. The system will affix your signature and the date to your online application. After you submit your application, petition, or request, you cannot make any changes.Pay the filing fee, if applicable.You must pay with a valid credit or debit card or provide your bank routing and checking account numbers to have money taken directly from your U.S. bank account.After you make your payment, your form will be submitted. If there is no fee associated with your application, then the form will be submitted directly to USCIS.For most forms, you will immediately receive a receipt notice that contains your receipt number. For some forms, it may take up to 3 days to receive a receipt number. A receipt number is a unique number that applies to your specific case with USCIS. You can find your receipt number on your online account home page, and you can find a copy of your receipt notice under the Documents or Notices tab, as applicable.View appointment notices.USCIS may schedule you for a biometric services appointment at an application support center. Log in to your USCIS online account for more information about your appointment.You must attend this appointment and provide biometric information, which may include your photograph, signature, and fingerprints.If you need to attend an interview, you will also receive an interview appointment notice in your account.Respond to Requests for Evidence and upload unsolicited evidence.USCIS will notify you by text message or email (based on your preference) if you need to respond to a Request for Evidence (RFE).Log in to your USCIS online account and go to the “Documents or Notices” tab, as applicable, to view notices and respond to the RFE.While your case is pending, you may provide additional information, including evidence USCIS did not specifically request, about your case. If you do not have an open RFE, you can do this in the “Documents or Evidence” tab, as applicable. Look for the additional evidence uploader at the bottom of the tab.Check the status of your case.Log in to your USCIS online account for details on the status of your case.Send and receive secure messages.After you file a form, you will have access to a secure inbox to send messages to USCIS and receive responses to your questions.Receive a decision.Log in to your USCIS online account to read details of the decision made on your case. For information on processing times for all forms, please visit our USCIS Processing Time Information page.
Article Summary: USCIS will soon mandate online filing for many immigration forms that have been available for e-filing for at least 180 days. The immigration authority shared a post on X (formerly Twitter) stating that “Digital submissions help us receive, store, and access information more efficiently”

Article Title: WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann says one car ride with SoftBank's Masayoshi Son set off WeWork's $47 billion collapse; the $4.2 billion deal signed on an iPad; the walk back to office when his ego took
Article Text:
Adam Neumann says a car ride with Masayoshi Son is where WeWork's $47 billion collapse began.

A 12-minute lobby chat with Masayoshi Son turned into a $4.2 billion SoftBank deal

Adam Neumann admits WeWork grew faster than he did

WeWork went from a $20 billion buyout offer to bankruptcy in five years

Adam Neumann is building Flow on the lessons of WeWork's fall

Work co-founder Adam Neumann says he can point to the exact moment his $47 billion company started to come apart, and it came years before the failed IPO. He traces it to a car ride through Manhattan with SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son in late 2016, a meeting of roughly half an hour that ended with a $4.2 billion investment offer signed on an iPad.Speaking to host Steven Bartlett on The Diary of a CEO podcast, in an episode released on September 28, Neumann said that deal changed how he saw his company. Son got out of the car near 54th Street, and Neumann walked the 36 blocks back to WeWork's headquarters. "Every step that I take, it goes higher and higher. And by the time I walk into HQ, 18th Street, I forgot what we were all about," he said. "It suddenly became about the money. "The night before, WeWork's board had agreed that Neumann would raise a modest $300 million to $400 million, slow down growth, turn a profit and then take the company public.Son, short on time before a meeting with then President-elect Donald Trump, spent just 12 minutes in WeWork's lobby before asking Neumann to keep talking in his car. The number started at 3billionandkeptclimbinguntilitreached"4.2 to be exact," as Neumann recalled on the podcast.Both men signed the terms on an iPad. SoftBank's investment, announced the following year, eventually totalled $4.4 billion.WeWork peaked at a $47 billion valuation after SoftBank added another $2 billion in January 2019. Losses kept piling up, including a $1.9 billion net loss for 2018.Neumann pointed to a flaw in the model: WeWork signed long leases in expensive cities and rented desks to members on short commitments. "We were taking long-term commitments against short-term commitments," he told Bartlett.He was just as blunt about himself. "Adam wasn't ready, and if the founder is not ready, the business is not ready," he said.Neumann also revisited a 2018 plan for SoftBank to buy WeWork outright at a $20 billion valuation. A special board committee pushed for $32 billion, and Son pulled out in December 2018 as SoftBank's own shares slid.When the IPO prospectus landed in August 2019, investors balked at the losses and Neumann's grip on control. The listing was shelved and he stepped down as CEO that September. He said he went "from 13,000 employees to three employees in one week."The pandemic emptied offices in 2020. WeWork filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in November 2023 with nearly $19 billion in debt. Neumann tried to buy it back in early 2024, but the company came out of bankruptcy without him.Now 47, Neumann says he measures success by how he expects to feel at the end of his life. Of the most successful people he knows, he said, "I have not seen one that got happy or fulfilled from attaining a number or a material thing."He is taking that thinking to Flow, the residential real estate startup he launched in 2022 to bring a sense of community to renting. On the podcast, Neumann said Andreessen Horowitz has invested $470 million in Flow across its Series A and B rounds, and his family has put in $350 million of its own. He added that Flow's software tracks profitability down to the building, floor and corner, something WeWork's systems never managed.Despite all of it, Neumann insists he has no regrets. "I am so happy that they happened because they made me exactly who I'm meant to be," he said of the hardest years. "Falling is not bad. The thing that's bad is not when you fall, it's how you get up."
Article Summary: WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann says he can point to the exact moment his $47 billion company started to come apart. He traces it to a car ride through Manhattan with SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son in late 2016. Neumann: "It suddenly became about the money"

Article Title: Accenture CEO Julie Sweet rejects concerns that AI is a threat to the company’s business model, says: Our strategy is to lean on ...
Article Text:
‘AI driving efficiency at Accenture, leading to bottomline growth’

Artificial intelligence is proving to be a dual engine for Accenture, driving customer demand while boosting internal productivity, CEO Julie Sweet announced during the company’s fourth-quarter earnings call. The Dublin-headquartered professional services giant reported that approximately 100 additional clients kicked off their first advanced AI projects in the fourth quarter. That pushed the total number of enterprise clients initiating advanced AI engagements with the firm past 400 for the fiscal year.Sweet once again rejected concerns that automation might undermine the traditional IT services model, describing AI efficiencies as a structural advantage rather than a business threat. “Our strategy is to lean into these efficiencies precisely because they create value for our clients while continuing to invest and rotate our capabilities to capture the larger growth opportunities AI creates,” Sweet said. “That is why we continue to view AI as a tailwind for Accenture.”The technology's momentum was reflected in fourth-quarter financial results. Accenture posted quarterly revenue of $18.7 billion, up 6 percent year-over-year, alongside new bookings of $22.2 billion, a 4 percent increase.For the full fiscal year, total revenue reached $74.2 billion, up by $4.5 billion. Investors responded swiftly to the earnings release, sending the company’s stock up more than 17 percent to trade around $214 on Thursday.“AI is now embedded across all of our work,” Sweet said on the call, noting that the company is integrating the technology early into client transformations spanning consulting, managed services, and ecosystem collaborations. “When you think about seven percent growth in every market, in consulting type of work, managed service and positive growth in every industry, the big growth drivers for the quarter were our large-scale reinventions, the ecosystem, and data and AI. ”Beyond driving client engagements, AI-driven automation is directly lifting Accenture’s bottom line. Sweet highlighted that productivity enhancements boosted revenue per employee in 2026, allowing the firm to execute larger, more complex projects without expanding headcount at the same rate as revenue growth. While Accenture plans to continue hiring across all global markets in 2027—including at entry levels, the overall pace of recruitment will moderate as automated systems absorb routine operational loads.This is not the first time that Accenture CEO has spoken about the company leaning heavily into AI. In March this year, while announcing the company's second quarter of Fiscal Year 2026, Sweet said, "We play a critical role in the AI ecosystem,” she said. “Our role is helping clients understand what to deploy and when, how to integrate it into their systems, reimagine their processes, modernize their data and digital core, and help build the capabilities and talent needed to scale across the enterprise. "“We see AI as a tailwind because it’s helping us win more today and take market share,” she said. “It is creating new opportunities for growth over time.”
Article Summary: Artificial intelligence is proving to be a dual engine for Accenture, driving customer demand while boosting internal productivity. The Dublin-headquartered professional services giant reported that approximately 100 additional clients kicked off their first advanced AI projects in the fourth quarter. The technology's momentum was reflected in fourth-quarter financial results.

Article Title: Elon Musk confirms talks with TSMC for Terafab chipmaking collaboration, says just discussions, but …
Article Text:
How the deal may work

Looming questions over Intel’s role

Elon Musk has confirmed that his companies are in active discussions with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) regarding a potential partnership for his Terafab semiconductor manufacturing. The confirmation comes as a report claimed that the talks explore establishing a dedicated chip manufacturing plant focused entirely on supplying Musk’s companies, including Tesla, SpaceX and artificial intelligence (AI) startup xAI.Musk acknowledged the engagement in a brief post on X (formerly Twitter), however, he downplayed anything concrete at the moment.“Just discussions, but something may come of it,” Musk wrote.He also replied, “True”, to a post which claimed that:“Anything TSMC contributes to Terafab would basically be supplemental. Terafab itself is going to be absurdly massive. The goal is 1 TW of compute production every year.....around 50× the current global output of AI compute. This isn’t just another fab. It’s being built for a scale the semiconductor industry simply does not operate at any known scale today.”Citing Tim Culpan’s Culpium newsletter which first claimed the potential collaboration, Tom’s Hardware reported that there may be two prospective operating models for the Terafab facility.Under the first plan, TSMC would directly own and run the fab. SpaceX or Terafab would contribute capital investments, sign binding minimum chip purchase agreements, or combine both commitments.Under the second plan, SpaceX may be granted majority control of the joint entity. TSMC would supply smaller capital injections while licensing proprietary process technologies and offering hands-on operational leadership.Background insights highlighted by Culpium suggest that persistent industry rumours regarding TSMC eyeing a chip fabrication complex in Texas may be closely linked to supporting the Terafab project.The emergence of TSMC may introduce major uncertainty around Intel's existing ties to Terafab. Currently, Intel is slated to deliver its 1.4-nanometer-class Intel 14A process node to manufacture semiconductors for SpaceX, Tesla and xAI under the Terafab banner. According to Tom’s Hardware, if TSMC secures an agreement to build and operate the facility using its own manufacturing nodes, Intel’s 14A technology could be pushed out of the equation entirely.
Article Summary: Elon Musk confirms talks with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) about Terafab semiconductor plant. Report claims that TSMC is interested in establishing a dedicated chip manufacturing plant focused entirely on supplying Musk’s companies, including Tesla, SpaceX and artificial intelligence (AI) startup xAI. Currently, Intel is slated to deliver its 1.4-nanometer-class Intel 14A process node to manufacture semiconductors for Musk's companies.

Article Title: Ten years on, every phone camera owes something to the Google Pixel
Article Text:
Google's Pixel taught phones how a photo should look.

One ordinary sensor was enough

Google taught software to do a lens's job

The trick didn't stay Google's for long

When software went a little too far

The Pixel look has started to wear thin

Every night photo on a modern phone looks a little brighter than the night it was taken in. Nobody complains, me included. We've grown so used to cameras that see more than our eyes can that a dark, grainy, faithful picture of a dark street now reads as a failure, something to delete and shoot again.That expectation didn't arrive on its own. A good part of it was built by a phone Google introduced in October 2016, with one camera on the back and a good deal of nerve, and the decade since has made the question it raised much louder. What is a phone photo supposed to look like?For most of the history of cameras, the answer was simple. Whatever was in front of the lens. Google has spent ten years rewriting that answer, and the rest of the industry has rewritten it right alongside.The first Pixel was not a remarkable-looking phone, and on paper its camera wasn't remarkable either: a 12.3-megapixel Sony sensor behind an f/2.0 lens, and no optical image stabilisation in a year when rivals considered it basic equipment. Apple put two lenses on the iPhone 7 Plus that same autumn. Google turned up to a hardware fight with a fairly regular camera, and kept much the same 12-megapixel sensor for its next four phones, betting that software could learn to do what the hardware couldn't.Then people started using it.The trick was HDR+, which Google had been refining since its Nexus phones in a team led by Marc Levoy, a Stanford professor who had taught computational photography long before the phrase meant much outside a lab. It wasn't AI in the sense anyone uses the word now, just a great deal of very clever maths. Press the shutter and the Pixel took a quick burst of deliberately dark frames, lined them up, and merged them into one image with clean shadows and a sky that hadn't burned out to white.You never saw any of that happen. You saw a friend in front of a bright window, and for once both the friend and the window looked right. Shot after shot came out that way, shadows lifted, highlights held, everything a touch contrasty, and before long people simply called it the Pixel look.That was enough to put a phone with an unremarkable sensor at the top of the camera rankings that year. The conversation had been about aperture numbers and pixel sizes for years, and here was a phone arguing, fairly convincingly, that what happened after the click mattered more. Machine learning took on more of that work with every Pixel that followed, years before anyone anyone could ask a chatbot how to fix a jammed film camera and be told to open the back.I wasn't old enough to need a phone of my own when that first Pixel showed up, and it took me until 2020 to get my first.The Pixel 2 took that argument somewhere more provocative. Portrait mode needed two cameras everywhere else in 2017, Apple included. Google did it with one, splitting each pixel on the sensor in two for a sliver of depth information and letting a machine learning model work out where a person ended and the background began.Stray hair went soft. Glasses occasionally dissolved into the blur. None of it stopped the point from landing: depth, once a property of glass and distance, could now be calculated. Google was sure enough of that to hold off on a second rear camera until the Pixel 4 in 2019, by which point most rival flagships carried three.My Pixel 2, already three years old by the time I got it, never had a second lens, and I never once wished it did. The photographer in me, the one with a big camera and a long lens, still bristles at software blur a little. Blur from a real lens is a consequence of physics. On the Pixel it became a decision the phone made for you, and most of the time it decided well.Night Sight, which arrived in late 2018 with the Pixel 3, is where most people felt the shift for themselves. Point the phone at a dim restaurant table, hold still for a few seconds, and it produced something your eyes hadn't quite registered. Colours you couldn't make out. Faces you could barely read.Huawei had shipped a handheld night mode earlier that year, to be fair, but Google pushed Night Sight to older Pixels through a software update, which said plenty about where the camera now lived. It's also why my Pixel 2 still held its own after dark right up to 2023, when phones around it were carrying three and even four lenses.The complaints were reasonable too. Some night shots looked like overcast afternoons, and Google spent the following years tuning shadow back in and shaving down the wait. On this year's Pixel 11 Pro, the wait is all but gone.Google had put a Night Sight shot beside a rival's on stage when it unveiled the Pixel 3, starting a ritual that hasn't let up since, and within a year the trick belonged to everyone. Apple answered with its own night mode and Deep Fusion on the iPhone 11, and Samsung's flagships were stacking frames for nearly every shot. Every one of them now faced the question Google had wrestled with first: how far a photo could drift from the moment before it stopped being that moment.What they borrowed most was the look. Shadows opened up, skies held their colour, faces stayed evenly lit against bright windows, and soon that HDR finish was simply what a good phone photo looked like, whoever made the phone.The borrowers didn't stop there. Huawei paired its processing with a periscope zoom on the P30 Pro, Xiaomi and Vivo moved to one-inch-type sensors, Vivo and Oppo built dedicated imaging chips, and Apple pushed its merging earlier in the pipeline with the Photonic Engine. Google had shown that software could rescue a small sensor, and its rivals were happy to show what the same thinking could do with a big one.Google followed eventually. The Pixel 6 arrived in 2021 with a large 50-megapixel sensor and Google's own Tensor chip, but the feature that probably mattered most barely made headlines. Real Tone set out to render darker skin accurately instead of washing it out, and got a fraction of the attention Night Sight had.Software that can calculate depth and pull colour out of the dark will, sooner or later, be asked to do more. With the Pixel 6, Google gave its camera Magic Eraser, and the drift Night Sight had raised as a worry became a feature. Tensor, Google said, was what made it possible, though the same eraser later ran happily on phones without one. Until then, everything the camera did worked on light that had actually reached the sensor. Now the stranger behind you on the beach could vanish, replaced by sand nobody had photographed.Each Pixel since has pushed further. Best Take built group shots where everyone happened to be smiling at once, and the Pixel 10 Pro's zoom started drawing in detail its lens could not resolve. I've yet to need a 100x photo of anything. It's the same confidence that once let one camera stand in for a portrait lens, now pointed at what's in the picture instead of how it's lit.The rest followed, not always gracefully. Huawei and Samsung both had to answer for moon shots that looked suspiciously better than their lenses allowed, Honor built a zoom that fills in what its telephoto can't see, and even Apple ships an eraser now.And don't even get me started on the generative tools. Magic Editor swaps in a new sky, Reimagine adds whatever you type, Add Me drops the person holding the phone into a group shot they were never in, and on the Pixel 10 you can just ask the Photos app to edit the picture for you. Google hands plenty of it to other Android phones and iPhones too. Somewhere around there, I stop being sure what a picture even is any more.Still, every one of those edits waits for you to ask, and they're a sliver of what anyone actually shoots. The birthday cake, the commute, the dog asleep on the sofa never get erased or reimagined; they just get processed, thousands of times over, with that same lifted, contrasty finish. That's AI too, just the quiet kind nobody bothers to call AI. I have three years of Pixel 2 photos that look exactly like that, and I didn't think twice about any of them. That's where the Pixel's influence runs deepest, and for years it was the part people thought about least. Then, slowly, they started to tire of it.Somewhere along the way, the look Google made famous turned into a uniform. By the end of the decade nearly every phone turned out the same evenly lit, shadowless, slightly too sharp picture by default. Line up the flagships I reviewed in any given month and you could have swapped their camera rolls without anyone noticing. That left phone makers with an awkward problem. If every camera's photos look alike, how do you sell yours?The Chinese went to the old names of photography, Huawei and later Xiaomi to Leica, Vivo to Zeiss, OnePlus and Oppo to Hasselblad, though what they hand you is mostly a fixed look picked from a menu. Google took longer, and by the time it moved, plenty of people had gone looking for character elsewhere, pulling cheap 2000s digicams out of drawers and chasing blown highlights and harsh flash through film presets. Even Levoy, now at Adobe, built Project Indigo to dial the processing back.Google's answer arrived this year as Camera Looks on the Pixel 11, and the difference is how far it lets you go. You pick a style before you shoot, Shadows for deeper contrast or Vanilla for something warmer, then pull warmth, highlights and saturation around until it's yours, and the image processor builds it into the shot instead of laying a filter over it.Google can't take all the credit, though. Apple got there first, answering years of complaints about over-processed iPhone photos with Photographic Styles in 2021, and it's the only other phone maker that hands over this much control. As for Google, even the name gives the game away. Camera Looks is aimed squarely at everyone who spent years grumbling about the Pixel look, and the plural is Google admitting there should never have been just one.A company that spent ten years deciding what your photos should look like is finally asking you.So what is a phone photo supposed to look like now? Ten years ago, Google's answer was the scene in front of you, rescued from a sensor too small to see it properly. Over a decade that slid into the scene as you'd have liked it, polished to a finish every phone maker copied until most people's photos stopped looking like their own. Generative AI is already pushing the answer somewhere new, into what belongs in the frame at all, but that's an argument for another day.On how a photo looks, every phone camera still makes most of the call for you, in milliseconds, before you've even looked at the screen. The Pixel is the reason they all do. Ten years on, it's also the phone handing a good part of that call back, letting a photo look warmer, moodier or a little worse if that's how you want it. For the phone that taught everyone to look past the sensor, I can't think of a better way to turn ten.
Article Summary: Google's first Pixel was not a remarkable-looking phone, and on paper its camera wasn't remarkable either. The trick was HDR+, which Google had been refining since its Nexus phones in a team led by Marc Levoy, a Stanford professor. It wasn't AI in the sense anyone uses the word now, just a great deal of very clever maths. The Pixel 2 took that argument somewhere more provocative.

Article Title: Tim Cook shares message on Steve Jobs’ death anniversary, says ‘he certainly changed my life forever’
Article Text:
Apple’s CEO John Ternus says he is 'forever grateful'

Tim Cook, former Apple CEO, shared a heartfelt tribute honouring the lasting imprint Steve Jobs left on technology and the people around him. On the occasion marking the 15th anniversary of the legendary Apple co-founder’s passing, Cook noted the personal and global difference his mentor made. In a post on X (formerly Twitter), Cook said that jobs not only changed the world and people but also had a positive impact on him. New company CEO John Ternus also shared a message, saying that he will be forever grateful for his contributions.“There are people who leave a mark on the world, and then there are people who change it entirely,” Cook wrote, adding, “Steve changed the world and so many lives in the process. He certainly changed my life forever. His spirit lives on in everything he created and everyone he inspired.”Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, also paid homage to the visionary leader, underscoring Jobs’ focus on design and the engineering philosophy he instilled across the company.“The way Steve taught us to care about every detail, every experience, every person, still guides our work today. Forever grateful,” Ternus stated.Jobs died at the age of 56 on October 5, 2011, following a battle with pancreatic cancer.His death occurred just 24 hours after Apple leadership stood on stage at the company’s Infinite Loop campus in Cupertino to announce the iPhone 4s. Shortly after Jobs’ death, Apple created a dedicated webpage titled "Remembering Steve" to house the massive wave of public condolences from across the globe.A decade and a half later, the company continues to host and maintain the live archive on its official website. The memorial showcases curated notes from over one million submissions sent in by customers, creators, and colleagues:“Over a million people from all over the world have shared their memories, thoughts, and feelings about Steve. One thing they all have in common — from personal friends to colleagues to owners of Apple products — is how they’ve been touched by his passion and creativity. You can view some of these messages below. And share your own at rememberingsteve@apple.com,” the tribute page reads.
Article Summary: Tim Cook, former Apple CEO, shared a heartfelt tribute honouring the lasting imprint Steve Jobs left on technology and the people around him. New company CEO John Ternus also shared a message, saying that he will be forever grateful for his contributions. Apple created a dedicated webpage titled "Remembering Steve" to house the massive wave of public condolences.

Article Title: In 2019, Alibaba Group co-founder Jack Ma told Elon Musk, 'Humans will always be smarter than machines': What Tesla CEO said
Article Text:
Ma says computer is one of clever tools humans created

At a time when there is an escalating debate over AI safety and the power of modern frontier models, an old video of an exchange between Elon Musk and Alibaba co-founder Jack Ma has surfaced online. The video, reposted by Musk, captures Ma doubling down on human exceptionalism, arguing that machines will never outsmart the species that invented them.“Computers may be very clever, but human beings are much smarter. We invented the computer. I've never seen a computer invent a human being,” Ma argued during their conversation at an event in Shanghai in 2019. Ma’s take was rooted in the traditional view of computing: machines are ultimately instruments. While hardware can compute equations faster and store far more data, people retain qualities that silicon cannot replicate, including life experience, nuanced judgment, and wisdom.Ma, however, acknowledged that AI can beat humans at games like chess and Go but said that computers would remain one of several clever tools that humans have developed.“Don't worry about the machines. For sure, we should understand one thing: that man can never make another man. A computer is a computer. A computer is just a toy. Man cannot even make a mosquito. So, we should have a confidence. Computers only have chips, men have the heart.It's the heart where the wisdom comes from,” he said.He concluded that “my view is that [a] computer may be clever, but human beings are much smarter”.Musk dismissed the premise immediately, posing a direct challenge: “What would be an example of something that humans are better than a computer at?”“It's going to get to the point where [AI] just can completely simulate a person in every way possible, like many people simultaneously. In fact, there's a strong argument, we're in the simulation right now," he added.
Article Summary: Alibaba co-founder Jack Ma and Tesla CEO Elon Musk had an exchange at an event in Shanghai in 2019. Ma argued that machines will never outsmart the species that invented them. Ma acknowledged that AI can beat humans at games like chess and Go but said computers would remain one of several clever tools that humans have developed.

Article Title: Anthropic admits to investors that the US government is a 'problem', says: We may experience business disruptions with ...
Article Text:
Anthropic

Existential risks and a 1% government revenue footprint

Anthropic has reportedly issued a warning to prospective investors that deteriorating relations with the US government and shifting political attitudes toward its technology may disrupt its commercial operations, sour partner relationships and trigger material revenue losses. The artificial intelligence (AI) startup made the blunt disclosure in its initial public offering (IPO) prospectus reviewed by news agency Reuters even as the company prepares for a high-profile public listing that could value the firm at roughly $2 trillion.The report said that while prospective public companies routinely warn that regulatory shifts could hurt procurement, Anthropic’s risk factors go far beyond typical vendor concerns. The company cautioned that negative perceptions of its technology and conduct risk spilling directly into the private sector, is shaking the confidence of corporate clients, platform partners, some employees and outside investors.According to the prospectus, such enforcement battles frequently bring “significant reputational harm, including adverse media coverage, public scrutiny, and negative perceptions among existing and prospective customers, partners, employees, and investors.”The filing concluded that pursuing government contracts carries inherent systemic volatility, noting that sudden shifts in how authorities view Anthropic or its underlying models can destabilise wider enterprise partnerships and cloud its long-term commercial roadmap.The prospectus presents a contradiction: a venture seeking multi-trillion-dollar market capitalisation on the promise of generative computing while warning that advanced models could ultimately pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”The company stressed that its exposure is not purely financial as direct federal work represents less than 1% of Anthropic’s annual top-line revenue. Rather, the hazard lies in political fallout, regulatory blowback and reputational damage. The tech company has become a regular in debates surrounding unchecked AI development, international rivalry and minimal regulatory oversight, the report pointed out.Public anxiety around frontier safety intensified after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged the tech sector to curb its development pace following repeated reports of cyber intrusions linked to rogue autonomous AI systems.Amodei had dinner with President Donald Trump last week as political demands for legal guardrails mounted. While Trump has largely dismissed appeals for strict federal curbs, the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is pressing forward with an industrywide investigation into leading AI labs, including Anthropic.
Article Summary: Anthropic is preparing for a high-profile public listing that could value the firm at roughly $2 trillion. The company cautioned that negative perceptions of its technology and conduct risk spilling directly into the private sector. Anthropic stressed that its exposure is not purely financial as direct federal work represents less than 1% of Anthropic’s annual top-line revenue.

Article Title: As October 5, 2026 marks the 15th Anniversary of Steve Jobs' death; here's the page that Apple has maintained in Jobs' memory since past 15 years
Article Text:
Photo: @readswithravi/ X

Remembering Steve Jobs' legacy: From Tim Cook to John Ternus

Fifteen years after Steve Jobs lost his battle with pancreatic cancer at the age of 56, the legacy of Apple ’s legendary co-founder continues to resonate across the tech landscape. Jobs passed away on October 5, 2011, just one day after Apple executives took the stage at the company’s Infinite Loop headquarters to unveil the iPhone 4s. The timing marked a poignant transition for the Silicon Valley giant, bridging the final chapter of Jobs’s hands-on leadership with the era that followed.In the days immediately after his death, Apple launched the 'Remembering Steve' webpage to host an outpouring of global tributes. A decade and a half later, the company still maintains the digital memorial, curating selections from more than one million messages submitted by admirers worldwide who shared their memories, reflections, and grief. One thing they all have in common — from personal friends to colleagues to owners of Apple products — is how they’ve been touched by his passion and creativity.You can view some of these messages below. And share your own at rememberingsteve@apple.com," reads the page's description.Apple is expected to commemorate the anniversary of co-founder Steve Jobs’ passing today, continuing the long-standing corporate tradition of public tributes and internal memorials. On the first anniversary of Jobs' death, the tech giant dedicated its homepage to a photo and audio slideshow celebrating his life and legacy. Throughout his tenure as Apple CEO, Tim Cook routinely marked the date by sharing public reflections on social media and sending internal memos to employees honoring Jobs' vision. With John Ternus now at the helm as Apple's new CEO, attention turns to whether the company's new leadership will continue the same public tradition.On Steve Jobs' first death anniversary, Tim Cook wrote, "Steve’s passing one year ago today was a sad and difficult time for all of us. I hope that today everyone will reﬂect on his extraordinary life and the many ways he made the world a better place. One of the greatest gifts Steve gave to the world is Apple. No company has ever inspired such creativity or set such high standards for itself. Our values originated from Steve and his spirit will forever be the foundation of Apple. We share the great privilege and responsibility of carrying his legacy into the future. I’m incredibly proud of the work we are doing, delivering products that our customers love and dreaming up new ones that will delight them down the road. It’s a wonderful tribute to Steve’s memory and everything he stood for."
Article Summary: Apple is expected to commemorate the anniversary of co-founder Steve Jobs’ passing today. Jobs passed away on October 5, 2011, just one day after Apple unveiled the iPhone 4s. In the days immediately after his death, Apple launched the 'Remembering Steve' webpage to host an outpouring of global tributes.

Article Title: Bill Gates bought a rare Porsche 959 but could not legally drive it in America; the car spent 13 years in customs
Article Text:
Why Bill Gates’ Porsche 959 was stuck in US customs

Porsche 959 was far ahead of its time

Only 292 road-going 959s were built

How Gates and other owners fought for a solution

What the Show or Display rule allowed

The Porsche 959 was born from rally racing

The 959 influenced later Porsche cars

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates bought a Porsche 959 in 1988, but the rare supercar could not legally be driven on US roads because it had not been certified under American safety and emissions rules. Instead, the car was held in a US customs facility for more than 13 years while Gates and other enthusiasts sought a way to legally import such rare vehicles. The 959 was among Porsche’s most technologically advanced cars of the 1980s, featuring a twin-turbocharged flat-six engine, all-wheel drive and advanced suspension. Gates’ car eventually benefited from the US “Show or Display” exemption, which allowed historically or technologically significant vehicles to be imported under strict conditions.The problem was not that the Porsche 959 was considered unsafe in the ordinary sense. Rather, it had not been certified to meet the US Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and emissions requirements needed for normal importation and registration. Porsche had built the 959 in very limited numbers and did not produce a US-certified version. As a result, Gates could own the car but could not simply register it and drive it on American roads.His 959 was subsequently held by US Customs for years while efforts were made to find a legal solution. According to Forbes, the car remained in customs for 4,745 days, or more than 13 years. The prolonged storage reportedly cost Gates about $133,000 in fees.The 959 was developed from Porsche’s work on the Group B rally programme and was intended to showcase advanced automotive technology. Porsche introduced the road-going version in the 1980s, making it one of the most sophisticated performance cars of its era. The car used a 2.85-litre flat-six engine with sequential twin turbochargers and produced around 450 PS. Porsche says it could reach a top speed of about 317 km/h and accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in 3.7 seconds. Its technology extended well beyond the engine. The 959 featured an advanced all-wheel-drive system, electronically controlled suspension, ABS and lightweight materials, technologies that were unusual in a production sports car at the time.The Porsche was also exceptionally rare. Porsche says only 292 road-going customer examples were produced between 1987 and 1988. The car originally cost around $225,000, making it extraordinarily expensive for its time. Its rarity and technological importance have since turned it into a highly sought-after collector car, with Porsche noting that examples have sold for more than $1.5 million at auction. Gates was not the only famous person to own one. Porsche lists comedian Jerry Seinfeld and tennis star Martina Navratilova among other notable 959 owners.Gates was not alone in facing the problem. Other American enthusiasts also wanted to own rare foreign vehicles that had never been certified for the US market. Automotive entrepreneur and Porsche specialist Bruce Canepa became particularly involved in efforts to create a legal route for such cars. Canepa had purchased a Porsche 959 and worked on making the model compliant with US requirements. The campaign eventually contributed to the creation of the Show or Display exemption, which provided a route for certain historically or technologically significant vehicles that did not meet all normal federal safety requirements.The exemption, which took effect in the late 1990s, allowed qualifying vehicles to enter the US under restrictions rather than being treated like ordinary imported cars. One major restriction was the mileage limit. Vehicles imported under the exemption generally could not be driven more than 2,500 miles per year. The cars also had to be considered sufficiently significant because of their historical or technological importance. Approval under the rule did not mean every other federal requirement, including applicable emissions requirements, automatically disappeared. For rare cars such as the Porsche 959, however, the provision created a legal pathway that had previously been unavailable.The 959's roots can be traced to Porsche’s participation in Group B rallying. The company used the programme to develop technologies that eventually appeared in the road-going 959. Porsche says the earlier competition version won the 1984 Paris-Dakar Rally, while Porsche achieved a one-two finish in the 1986 event. The rally programme also helped Porsche develop the sophisticated four-wheel-drive technology that became one of the defining features of the 959.The 959's significance extended beyond its rarity and performance. Porsche says its development demonstrated the advantages of combining high performance with all-wheel drive and advanced electronic systems. The company later used lessons from the 959 in other performance models. Porsche has described the 959 as a catalyst for its decision to equip future turbocharged sports cars with all-wheel drive.
Article Summary: The Porsche 959 was among Porsche’s most technologically advanced cars of the 1980s. It featured a twin-turbocharged flat-six engine, all-wheel drive and advanced suspension. Only 292 road-going customer examples were produced between 1987 and 1988. The car originally cost around $225,000, making it extraordinarily expensive.
