Article Title: Equinix data center spills thousands of gallons of diesel in Hackensack River; New Jersey Mayor attributes it to a 'computer glitch', department claims no observed impacts on local wildlife
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representation

Thousands of gallons of diesel spilled

Mayor cites a computer glitch

“We regret that this occurred and the concern it has caused the community,”

Equinix has faced a previous spill

Why data centers use diesel

A New Jersey data center has spilled thousands of gallons of diesel fuel into a tributary of the Hackensack River. This has prompted a cleanup operation and questions about how the leak occurred. The company has confirmed that the spill happened last month at Equinix’s NY2 facility in Secaucus. Equinix said its operations staff detected a fuel release from a storage tank outside the building, stopped the leak and brought in Clean Harbors to begin remediation.According to a report by New Jersey News 12, Secaucus Mayor Michael Gonnelli initially attributed the incident to a “computer glitch”, while Equinix said two broken valves caused the release. The company also said it contacted the Secaucus Fire Department, which responded and notified the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection and the Hudson Regional Health Commission.The NJDEP said the 5,000-gallon spill originated from a storage tank at the Equinix data center in Secaucus. Fuel flowed into an unnamed tributary of the Hackensack River, although officials said it did not reach the river itself.A cleanup operation over the weekend removed much of the fuel. Crews had recovered about 3,500 gallons and continued removing fuel from affected areas of the creek.The department said the spill had not resulted in any observed impacts on local wildlife. It also said no drinking water intakes were near the affected area.Secaucus Mayor Michael Gonnelli initially described the incident as the result of a “computer glitch” in comments to local news outlets. He said the data center, which has operated at the site since 2001, had not previously experienced a similar issue.Equinix, however, provided a different explanation. The company said the spill resulted from two broken valves used during the facility's routine filtration process and that it was preparing a full incident response report.the statement said.The incident is not the first diesel spill involving a data center in New Jersey. In 2017, about 600 gallons of fuel from a data center entered storm drains in the Clifton area. In 2022, an Equinix data center in North Bergen spilt about 1,800 gallons of diesel.The latest incident therefore involves a larger volume of fuel than those previous cases. Data centre-related diesel spills have also been reported elsewhere in the US, although they represent a small share of overall oil spills.Diesel fuel is commonly used to power backup generators at data centers. These generators keep facilities operating during power outages, when interruptions can affect the services hosted inside.The use of backup diesel generators has expanded alongside data center construction. According to the Better Data Center Project, data center diesel generator capacity increased from 20 gigawatts in 2018 to 55 gigawatts in 2024.Data centers also require substantial cooling infrastructure, which can lead to facilities being built near water sources. That can create additional environmental concerns when fuel or other materials escape from a facility.
Article Summary: Thousands of gallons of diesel spilled into a tributary of the Hackensack River. The company has confirmed that the spill happened last month at Equinix’s NY2 facility in Secaucus. Secaucus Mayor Michael Gonnelli initially attributed the incident to a “computer glitch”, while EquinIX said two broken valves caused the release.

Article Title: Billionaire David Sacks hits at Bill Gates over his comments that AI will cause billion deaths; fires a 'Chinese question' at him
Article Text:
What David Sacks said about Gates’ AI warning

Bill Gates says AI can already help bioterrorists and hackers

American billionaire David Sacks has criticised Bill Gates over his warning that artificial intelligence could become powerful enough to cause events resulting in a billion deaths. David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI czar, reposted clips on X (formerly Twitter) challenging Bill Gates’ comments and questioning how the US could prevent Chinese AI models from developing similar capabilities. One clip attributed to Sacks says, “There are no facts or evidence to justify these types of numbers.” In another reposted clip, Sacks raised the issue of AI development in China. “The question I have for Bill [Gates] is, how are you going to stop Chinese models from developing these capabilities?” he said.Speaking during an interview with NBC’s Meet the Press, Bill Gates said that AI is “certainly powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths.” Gates also called for mandatory federal legislation to address AI risks. He argued that the technology should not be governed only through voluntary industry rules and urged Congress to take action, although he did not identify a specific bill.David Sacks responded by reposting clips of Gates’ remarks on X. In one clip, he questioned the basis for putting such a large number on the potential death toll. “There are no facts or evidence to justify these types of numbers,” the clip attributed to Sacks says.Sacks’ comments come as the US and China compete to develop increasingly advanced AI systems.Recently, Bill Gates was asked why product liability and reputational damage aren't enough to stop firms from releasing dangerous AI. During his appearance at the Ezra Klein Show, Gates answered with a question of his own. “So say you kill 100 million people, you want to use a lawsuit?” adding “I almost can't keep a straight face.”Host Ezra Klein put to Gates a view voiced by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: if a product is unsafe, the CEO simply shouldn't launch it, and no new laws are needed. Klein added that Trump and David Sacks, who has advised the President on AI, hold a similar position.Gates disagreed. He said AI can already help a bioterrorist kill hundreds of millions of people, or carry out a cyberattack that scrambles bank accounts and shuts down a power grid. "We crossed the cyber threshold and we crossed the bio threshold early this year," he said.
Article Summary: Gates said AI can already help a bioterrorist kill hundreds of millions of people, or carry out a cyberattack that scrambles bank accounts and shuts down a power grid. David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI czar, reposted clips of Gates’ remarks on X (formerly Twitter)

Article Title: In 2003, Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen committed $100 million to brain research; three years later, his institute completed a mouse brain gene atlas and made it freely available online
Article Text:
​In 2003, Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen committed $100 million to brain research

Why did Paul Allen invest $100 million in brain research

What was the Allen Brain Atlas

Allen Brain Atlas mapped more than 21,000 genes

Microsoft co-founder Paul G. Allen committed $100 million to brain research in 2003, funding the creation of the Allen Institute for Brain Science in Seattle. Its first major project was the Allen Brain Atlas, an effort to map gene activity across the mouse brain. Three years later, the institute announced the completion of the atlas, creating a detailed, three-dimensional map covering more than 21,000 genes at the cellular level. As listed on the website, the data was made publicly available online at no cost, giving scientists around the world access to information that could help them study the brain and disorders including Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, epilepsy, schizophrenia and autism.Paul Allen said he had become increasingly interested in genomics and neuroscience and wanted to understand how the brain works.“Over the last decade I have become increasingly interested in the fields of genomics and neuroscience, and their important role in human development, behavior, and health – and ultimately, understanding more about how the brain actually works,” Allen said in 2003.The Allen Institute was created as a private nonprofit organisation, with the aim of supporting research into areas including cognition, language, emotion and memory.Allen institute's first project was designed to show which genes are active in different parts of the mouse brain. The project combined neuroscience and genomics to create a molecular map of the brain. Scientists could use the information to study how genes relate to different brain regions and functions.The mouse was chosen because it has long been used in biomedical research and shares more than 90% of its genes with humans, according to the institute.When the project was completed, the Atlas contained information on more than 21,000 genes at the cellular level. The institute said the Atlas showed that about 80% of genes are active in the brain, higher than the 60% to 70% scientists had previously believed.“This project is an unprecedented union of neuroscience and genomics,” Allen said. The Atlas was made publicly available at no cost, allowing researchers to access the data online. Harvard professor Catherine Dulac called it “an enormous mine of information” and said its immediate public availability was “absolutely tremendous.”The project was already attracting more than 4 million hits a month before its completion and was being accessed by about 250 scientists on a typical work day. Stanford professor Ben A. Barres, who used the Atlas in his research, said: “It’s completely essential. It’s saved us years and years of work, maybe decades.”The institute later planned to shift its focus toward human brain research and studies of neurological and psychiatric disorders.
Article Summary: Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen committed $100 million to brain research in 2003. Allen Institute for Brain Science's first project was to map gene activity across the mouse brain. Three years later, the institute announced the completion of the atlas, creating a detailed, three-dimensional map covering more than 21,000 genes at the cellular level.

Article Title: Apple has had no design chief since Jony Ive left, so CEO John Ternus is doing the job himself
Article Text:
Apple CEO John Ternus displays the iPhone Duo on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, on the Apple campus in Cupertino, Calif. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)

Ternus spends far more time in Apple's design studio than Tim Cook did

Apple has gone without a single design head since Jony Ive's exit in 2019

Apple is rebuilding its design team rather than hiring a new design chief

Apple CEO John Ternus has quietly taken on a second job. About a month after succeeding Tim Cook, Ternus has made himself the company's de facto design chief, overseeing both the industrial design team that shapes Apple 's hardware and the human interface team behind its software. Nobody at Apple has held that combined role since Jony Ive left in 2019.The detail comes from Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, who writes in his Power On newsletter that Ternus works hands-on in the design studio several times a week, sometimes dropping in more than once a day. Apple is not looking for an outside chief design officer either. For a company whose identity is tied so closely to how its products look and feel, that makes the new CEO the final word on design, much as Steve Jobs was.The contrast with the Cook era is sharp. Designers cited in the report say Cook typically spent about an hour in the studio once a month, at most. His tenure leaned on operations, sales, the supply chain and Apple's dealings with governments.Ternus is splitting the job differently. Finance now sits largely with CFO Kevan Parekh and the supply chain with COO Sabih Khan. That frees Ternus, a hardware engineer and 25-year Apple veteran, to work closely with chief hardware officer Johny Srouji and hardware engineering head Tom Marieb, while spending serious time with designers.He has explained the shift to employees through an early conversation with Cook. When Ternus told his predecessor he wasn't him, Cook's reply was blunt: "I know you're not me." Ternus took it to mean he should spend his time where he adds the most value.After Ive left, industrial design and human interface got separate leaders who reported to former COO Jeff Williams, a manufacturing specialist with no design background. When Williams retired in 2025, Apple said design would report to Cook. In practice, the teams answered to Ternus, who was made the internal "executive sponsor" of design ahead of the CEO handover. Between April and September, the design leaders were effectively his only direct reports.The studio he inherited had thinned out. Designers left for Ive's firm LoveFrom and OpenAI's hardware group, among others. Software design chief Alan Dye moved to Meta, and Ive's successor Evans Hankey eventually joined OpenAI. Molly Anderson, who had never managed a team of this size, became vice president of industrial design in 2024. Apple had to promote junior designers and hire heavily from outside.Ternus has made restoring the studio's standing an early priority. Apple put Anderson and Steve Lemay, Dye's successor, front and centre during the iPhone Duo launch, with Ternus posing alongside Anderson and the new foldable. This past week, the company also hired Belgian furniture designer Julien Renault.Whether an engineer can fill the space Ive left behind remains an open question. What is clear is that design once again has a direct line to the CEO's office, and the first real tests are close. The first products to reach buyers under this setup are close: Apple's smart home hub is set to be unveiled on October 13, the iPhone Duo goes on sale later this month, and a lighter MacBook Pro with an OLED touch screen is expected to follow next month. The weight cut comes from inside, where Apple has reportedly shrunk parts and rearranged components.
Article Summary: Apple has gone without a single design head since Jony Ive's exit in 2019. Apple is not looking for an outside chief design officer either. For a company whose identity is tied so closely to how its products look and feel, that makes the new CEO the final word on design.

Article Title: One of America's biggest investor Michael Burry tells Wall Street to not allow OpenAI and Anthropic IPO, warns: These are companies that are going to destroy TRILLIONS of dollars of capital
Article Text:
The financial case behind the warning from Michael Burry

Not his first AI warning, and not his only bearish bet

AI labs themselves aren't entirely dismissive of the risk

Michael Burry, America’s biggest investor, who is best known for predicting and profiting from the 2008 housing market collapse, has now warned that public listings by AI giants Sam Altman-led OpenAI and Anthropic could lead to massive capital destruction, arguing that the companies should be prevented from going public. In a post shared by on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Burry said that markets should ‘tank hard’ in order to stop the planned initial pubic offerings (IPOs) of OpenAI and Anthropic, describing such an outcome as being ‘for the benefit of humanity’. He later expanded on his criticism, claiming the two companies would ‘suck up’ and then destroy ‘TRILLIONS of dollars of capital’. According to Burry, the financial losses would be "the least of the damage they do."Burry's latest remarks come as both companies edge closer to the public markets, each carrying enormous capital requirements alongside rapid growth. Anthropic's confidential IPO prospectus, reviewed by Reuters, revealed at least $518 billion in future cloud, computing, and infrastructure commitments, with the company potentially seeking a valuation above $2 trillion when it lists. OpenAI confidentially filed its own draft registration statement in June, though CEO Sam Altman has said this isn't the right time to list, and the company is now reportedly aiming for a 2027 debut instead.Burry's core argument centers on a mismatch he sees between the scale of capital being poured into these companies and how proven their underlying economics actually are — essentially questioning who ends up absorbing the losses if AI revenue growth fails to keep pace with the enormous infrastructure spending required to sustain it.This latest broadside is part of a broader pattern for Burry, who has grown increasingly bearish on the AI sector over the past year. His bearish positions have included bets against Nvidia, Palantir, Micron, Oracle, and the Nasdaq 100, built around a thesis that borrowing-driven investment in semiconductors and data infrastructure can't be sustained indefinitely, and would be especially vulnerable if interest rates rise.Interestingly, OpenAI and Anthropic have both acknowledged, at least to some degree, the dangers posed by their own technology. Anthropic's confidential draft prospectus reportedly acknowledged that its AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risk to humanity — though such disclosures are standard practice in IPO risk-factor sections, intended to flag potential risks to investors rather than an admission that these outcomes are likely or imminent.His X posts followed a Substack newsletter he published the same day in which he said he was more confident than ever that his bearish AI thesis would play out within the next year — notably moving up his own previous timeline, which had placed 2028 as his base-case scenario for when the AI bubble would burst.
Article Summary: Michael Burry, America's biggest investor, has warned that public listings by AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic could lead to massive capital destruction. In a post shared by on social media platform X, Burry said that markets should ‘tank hard’ in order to stop the planned initial pubic offerings. He later expanded on his criticism, claiming the two companies would ‘suck up’ and then destroy ‘TRILLIONS of dollars of capital’

Article Title: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg told his 7-year-old daughter: You do not have this Taylor Swift option
Article Text:
Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan

What Mark Zuckerberg told his daughter about Taylor Swift

What Mark Zuckerberg’s daughter said

Mark Zuckerberg’s daughter can’t vibe code products "open to the internet"

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg once had an unusual message for his young daughter after taking her to a Taylor Swift concert: she could admire the pop star, but she could not simply choose to become her. In a clip going viral on the internet, Mark Zuckerberg recalled the conversation with his daughter August Chan Zuckerberg on the Acquired podcast, saying the then-7-year-old told him she wanted to be like Swift when she grew up. In the video, Zuckerberg said that he told her that option was not available to her. August, however, quickly turned the conversation into her own ambition, saying she wanted people to want to be like her when she grew up.Mark Zuckerberg said he had taken August to a Taylor Swift concert. After the show, she told him she wanted to be like the singer when she became an adult.“One day my daughter, we took her to a Taylor Swift concert, and she was like, ‘You know, Dad, I kind of want to be like Taylor Swift when I grow up,’” Zuckerberg said.His response was direct. “I was like, ‘But you can't, that's not available to you.’”The conversation took place sometime in 2024, when August was around seven years old.Rather than being discouraged, August came up with a different goal. “She thought about it and she's like, ‘All right, when I grow up, I want people to want to be like August Chan Zuckerberg,’” Zuckerberg recalled. Her response appeared to please her father.“And I was like, ‘Hell yeah!’” he said.August has also been exploring technology on her own. In a profile of Priscilla Chan and Zuckerberg, Chan showed journalist Jeremy Stern some of her daughter's creations on Replit, a platform used for coding. Priscilla Chan said her daughter had created projects including a messaging app and apps similar to GeoCities and FarmVille. The projects also included marketing and sales plans.However, Chan said she limits what her daughters can make available online. “She's quite limited, because Mom doesn't let her build things that are open to the internet,” Chan said.“She wanted to build a dating site,” Chan said. “That was a no.”Mark Zuckerberg had previously said in 2024 that one of his daughters was 40 pages into writing a novel about “mermaid crystals” with AI-generated images. Chan also stressed that the coding projects were not something Zuckerberg had pushed his daughter to do.“He didn't tell her to do any of this,” Chan said. “It's been all on her own,” she added.
Article Summary: Mark Zuckerberg said he had taken August Chan Zuckerberg to a Taylor Swift concert. After the show, she told him she wanted to be like the singer when she became an adult. August has also been exploring technology on her own. Priscilla Chan said she limits what her daughters can make available online.

Article Title: Intel co-founder Gordon Moore paid $6 million for this 25-acre California estate in 1991; his former home is now listed for $29.5 million with protected land
Article Text:
PC: WSJ

Gordon Moore bought the Woodside estate for $6 million in 1991

A 1920s manor house retained its original character

PC: WSJ

The Woodside estate expanded with gardens and a second house

The conservation easement changed the future of the land

From a $6 million purchase to a $29.5 million listing

In 1991, Gordon Moore paid about $6 million for a large property in Woodside, California, adding a substantial private estate to the life of one of Silicon Valley’s best-known figures. Almost three decades later, Moore’s estate placed the property under a permanent conservation easement, limiting what could be built or changed across the site.According to The Wall Street Journal 2025 reports, the property was listed for $29.5 million, covers about 25 acres and includes an English Manor-style house dating to around 1927. There are gardens, redwood groves, walking trails, a creek and an old apple orchard, along with several buildings and recreational facilities. It is also surrounded by the Golden Gate National Recreation Area, giving the estate a setting that is unusually open for a property in the wealthy San Francisco Peninsula community.Moore and his wife, Betty, acquired the Woodside property in 1991 for roughly $6 million. At the time, Moore was already an important figure in the technology industry. He had co-founded Intel with Robert Noyce in 1968, and his observation about the growth in transistor numbers later became known as Moore’s Law.The couple remained connected to the Woodside estate for more than three decades. The property eventually became part of Moore’s estate, with the Peninsula Open Space Trust taking responsibility for selling it after his death.At the centre of the property is an English Manor-style residence built around 1927. The main house measures about 9,300 square feet and contains six bedrooms. Rather than replacing its older character, the Moores spent years updating the infrastructure while retaining parts of the original design.Their work included replacing the electrical, plumbing and heating and cooling systems. The kitchen was enlarged, but features such as redwood panelling and five wood-burning fireplaces remained. An old call-button system, originally used by household staff, was also restored.There is even a vault in the butler’s pantry. It dates from the property's earlier history, when previous owners used it to keep valuables. A spiral staircase rises to a loft with cathedral ceilings, where he displayed fossils, mineral specimens and vintage fishing reels.The Moores added a separate caretakers’ residence in 1994, measuring roughly 2,500 square feet, as reported by WSJ. Four bedrooms are located there, bringing the total number of bedrooms across the two homes to 10.Outside, the property is spread across a mixture of landscaped and more natural areas. There is a swimming pool and tennis court, as well as a greenhouse associated with Betty Moore’s gardening. The grounds include a rose garden, redwood stands, walking trails and a creek. A century-old apple orchard is also part of the estate.Three garages and other outbuildings add to the collection of structures. Despite its size, the property has remained tied to a landscape where much of the surrounding land is protected from intensive development.The most significant long-term restriction on the property is its conservation easement. The easement prevents large-scale development, meaning the land cannot simply be treated as an unrestricted parcel for future construction.That protection is particularly relevant because the property sits in Woodside, around 30 miles south of downtown San Francisco, in an area where large estates command high prices. The conservation arrangement places a limit on how the acreage can be developed even as ownership changes.Moore’s estate left the property to the Peninsula Open Space Trust, which is marketing the home. The trust’s president, Gordon Clark, said the Moores had spent about $15 million renovating and improving the property during their ownership while paying close attention to the original structure.The result is a property that carries two very different kinds of value. There is the house itself, with its period features and extensive grounds, and there is the land, much of which is subject to a permanent restriction on large-scale development.The property is currently listed for $29.5 million, almost five times the approximately $6 million the Moores paid for it in 1991. The listing is being handled by Hugh Cornish of Coldwell Banker Realty and Erika Demma of Compass.According to The Wall Street Journal, the community’s most expensive home sale the previous year reached $52 million. Cornish said demand had increased as affluent buyers from San Francisco looked for weekend properties outside the city.The Moores had another significant property in Hawaii. That home was listed for $28.8 million in February and was later reduced to $21.9 million. Gordon Moore died in March 2023 at the age of 94. Betty Moore died later that year at 95. Their long ownership of the Woodside estate ended with the property passing into the care of a conservation organisation, rather than simply becoming another unrestricted development site.
Article Summary: Gordon Moore bought the Woodside estate for $6 million in 1991. It includes an English Manor-style house dating to around 1927. There are gardens, redwood groves, walking trails, a creek and an old apple orchard, along with several buildings and recreational facilities.

Article Title: Airtel launches IQ Gateway to bring SMS, WhatsApp, RCS and voice on one enterprise platform
Article Text: Airtel Business launched Airtel IQ Gateway, which it describes as India's first business communications platform powered by telco-grade network intelligence, aimed at helping enterprises manage customer interactions across multiple channels while reducing fraud and delivery failures. The new platform brings together SMS, WhatsApp, Rich Communication Services (RCS), business voice communications and number verification capabilities on a single DPDP-compliant control plane. Airtel said the offering is designed to help enterprises simplify customer engagement while improving security and regulatory compliance.According to Airtel Business, organisations often rely on multiple vendors and communication tools to reach customers, creating operational complexity and limited visibility into message delivery. The company said Airtel IQ Gateway enables enterprises to manage all customer communication channels from a unified dashboard with real-time analytics and delivery reporting. The platform also supports automatic switching to backup service providers and intelligent routing across communication channels. Airtel said the platform is particularly relevant for industries such as banking, financial services, government, e-commerce and logistics, where secure customer communications are critical.The platform includes Airtel IQ Verify, a fraud-scoring system that evaluates network, device and usage signals to detect suspicious account creation attempts, account takeovers and artificial traffic spikes. Airtel said the feature can help enterprises reduce losses linked to fraud and inflated messaging traffic. The company also highlighted protection against fraudulent SMS pumping, a practice where bots generate artificial international OTP traffic, increasing communication costs for enterprises.In addition, the platform offers Silent Authentication, which validates whether a mobile number matches the active SIM card in a user's device. Airtel said this can reduce dependence on OTP-based login systems and help mitigate SIM-swap and social engineering risks.Airtel IQ Gateway can be deployed either on an enterprise's premises or through Airtel's cloud infrastructure as a software-as-a-service (SaaS) offering, depending on security and operational requirements. The company said the platform also automates integration with Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT)-based messaging systems and helps businesses manage approved message templates more efficiently.Sharat Sinha, CEO of Airtel Business, said trusted digital interactions are becoming increasingly important as India expands its digital economy. "With IQ Gateway, we are extending this proven expertise to enterprises, enabling them to build brand trust while ensuring every customer conversation is safe, authenticated and resilient," Sinha said.Airtel said the platform has already undergone trials with select banks, financial institutions and industry partners before its nationwide launch.
Article Summary: Airtel Business launched Airtel IQ Gateway, which it describes as India's first business communications platform. The new platform brings together SMS, WhatsApp, Rich Communication Services (RCS), business voice communications and number verification capabilities on a single DPDP-compliant control plane.

Article Title: AWS CEO Matt Garman says data centers aren’t using as much water as claimed; debunks 4 ‘popular myths’; says ‘There are clearly …’
Article Text:
Here are data center myths debunked by AWS CEO Matt Garman

Myth #1: Data centers are taking all of our water

Myth #2: Data center providers are responsible for driving up all the energy rates

Myth #3: Data centers emit huge amounts of pollution with their large backup diesel generators

Myth #4: Community members get nothing from data centers

AWS CEO Matt Garman recently pushed back against growing criticism of data centers, calling four common claims about their impact “myths.” In a long blog post, Matt Garman addressed concerns over water consumption, rising electricity rates, pollution from backup diesel generators and the benefits data centers bring to local communities. He argued that data centers use far less water than often claimed, are not solely responsible for higher power bills and rarely run their backup generators. Garman also said data centers generate billions of dollars in tax revenue, create jobs and support schools, emergency services and other local projects in communities where they operate.“There are clearly areas in which the technology and energy industries can be doing better (along with their government partners) but just like in the past when the country has banded together to accomplish something that’s critical for our national security and economic prosperity—we should approach this as a long-term mission that the private and public sectors pursue together,” Garman said adding “Let’s start with some of the myths floating around”.This is false. Data centers actually use very little water relative to other industries. Direct data center water consumption is about 0.5% of total U.S. direct industrial water use—orders of magnitude less than golf courses, almond farming, and many other industries. For instance, U.S. golf courses alone use ~200x more water than all of Amazon’s data centers—more in about two days than we use in a full year. And, in a recent study of major U.S.industries that collectively account for ~50% of U.S. industrial GDP, data centers ranked lowest in water withdrawals while delivering the highest economic value per gallon.One of the most common soundbites repeated about water is that a typical data center uses five million gallons per day. This is also false. The reality is that a typical data center uses, on average, about 170,000 gallons per day. And at Amazon, our average data center uses less than 13,000 gallons per day (the equivalent of just 42 U.S. households).This is misleading and convenient scapegoating. First, the facts: if you look across states with large numbers of data centers, costs have gone up in some (e.g., Illinois, New York), down in some (e.g., Indiana and Mississippi), and grown slower than the national average in places like Texas. In instances where energy rates are going up, it’s primarily because the grid is old and hasn’t been invested in and expanded before the demand arrived. About 70% of the power lines were built over 25 years ago, with many dating back to the 1960s and 1970s. The capacity and performance needed hasn’t scaled with the rapid growth of digital and AI demand, and the accelerated adoption of AI is precipitating a build-out that was destined to happen—it’s just happening faster than most folks imagined. And, once we collectively build out this new capacity, again funded by the private sector, it should lead to flat or lower rates in the future for residents living in communities with these expanded grids, which we’re already seeing in some states such as Mississippi, Georgia, and Indiana. For our data centers, we work directly with utilities to understand the funds that are necessary to support our projects (e.g., new transmission lines, substations, and other grid upgrades) and then ensure that the revenue we provide to the utility is sufficient to pay for these requirements.This is also untrue. Most of the services consumers, businesses, and governments rely on every day (e.g., 911 calls, stock markets, healthcare and banking apps, ride-hailing apps like Uber and Lyft, ChatGPT) depend on data centers functioning. As a result, data centers have backup power available in case of a power outage. Some do this through diesel generators that sit idle most of the year. However, when those generators are installed, companies need to get permits for the full potential emissions—what those generators would produce if they ran for the maximum hours under the permit. Critics then see those permits and say things like “…the generators could emit up to 249.9 tons per year each of nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and volatile organic compounds.” The truth is data center generators almost never run. They’re idle 99.9% of the time (they run roughly 10 hours per year, mostly for required maintenance testing). And even when backup generators do run, much of the industry now uses Tier 4 emission controls (the cleanest EPA emission standard), so annual NOx emissions from an average data center are the same as a single round trip flight from Seattle to London.This is also false. Data centers bring considerable tax revenue, positive economic impact, large numbers of good jobs, education programs and other benefits to the communities where they’re built. Data center operators are often the single largest taxpayer in a community, with upfront payments routinely exceeding entire annual municipal budgets in the first year of construction, and long-term tax revenue often exceeding prior land use revenue by more than 1,000%. For example, in St. Joseph County, Indiana, the taxes Amazon will pay to the county are estimated to exceed $3 billion, while the prior use on the same land would have paid just $1.2 million over the same term. In Montgomery County, Missouri, our project will pay more than $1.8 billion in taxes over 25 years, while the prior use would have generated about $200,000 (0.01% of what we’ll pay in taxes) over the same period. A 2026 report by Mangum Economics for the Northern Virginia Technology Council estimates that without data center revenue, the average homeowner in Loudoun County, Virginia would pay additional property taxes of $5,800 per year.This new revenue from data centers often not only dramatically reduces the taxes paid by families, but it also funds investments in schools, fire and police departments, parks, roads, and other community services. This is on top of the direct investments most data center companies make to local organizations that are used to address issues most important to them, such as modernized emergency dispatch services, clean energy projects, and support for local food banks. Over the past three years, Amazon has contributed more than $1 billion to communities across the U.S. in which we have a meaningful data center presence.Additionally, thousands of construction jobs are created to build data centers. These jobs benefit families in these communities and are a boon for local small businesses. The average wages paid far exceed local and national medians, and the job numbers associated with these projects are typically very significant compared to the size of these communities. For example, in Madison County, Mississippi (population: 116,000), where we have two data center sites under construction, there are over 2,300 people currently employed in construction; and in Newton County, Georgia (population: 125,000), there are over 1,500 people currently employed. Many jobs are also created to operate a data center once it’s complete. For example, for the data centers in Madison County, we will employ over 1,700 people, and in Newton County, we will employ 400 people. And, we have over 20 education and workforce development programs to help ensure these jobs are available to people from the community, and over 10,000 learners and educators are participating in our programs across 15 data center regions. You can read more about those and our other education programs here.
Article Summary: AWS CEO Matt Garman addressed concerns over water consumption, rising electricity rates, pollution from backup diesel generators and the benefits data centers bring to local communities. Garman said data centers generate billions of dollars in tax revenue, create jobs and support schools, emergency services and other local projects in communities where they operate.

Article Title: LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman wants Americans to stop 'hating' datacentres; calls them the only reason US is not in a recession
Article Text:
Reid Hoffman defends AI infrastructure boom

Context: a boom not without controversy

Not everyone shares Reid Hoffman's optimism

LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman has defended the massive wave of AI infrastructure investment in the United States, arguing that spending on data centers and related projects is providing a significant boost to the broader economy and helping the country to avoid recession. According to a report by Benzinga, speaking on the Newcomer podcast, Hoffman said that billions of dollars flowing into AI infrastructure are generating economic activity far beyond technology companies. According to him, the current AI buildout is ‘the only reason we’re not in recession’, highlighting the role of a large-scale capital investments in supporting jobs and growth. He pushed back on the common perception that this investment narrowly benefits only tech companies, arguing that most of that capital doesn't actually concentrate in the specific areas where data centers are physically built, but instead ends up more broadly distributed across the country — a dynamic he described as a clear positive.Reid Hoffman emphasized the ripple effects this spending has on local economies, pointing to the range of workers who benefit from data center construction beyond the tech industry itself: construction workers, carpenters, real estate agents, electricians, and lawyers, among others. He argued that people tend to assume this capital infusion flows exclusively to tech companies, when in reality a massive percentage of it is actually going toward the physical work of building data centers themselves.Hoffman also said data center developers have a responsibility to work fairly with the local communities hosting these projects, framing it as essential that both developers and communities come away benefiting from the arrangement, rather than one side absorbing most of the costs or disruption.Hoffman's defense of data center spending comes amid a broader wave of scrutiny over how AI infrastructure investment is being financed and accounted for. Earlier this month, Meta reportedly classified some of its AI data centers as "pilot models" in order to claim federal research tax credits, a move that reduced the company's 2025 tax bill by $3.9 billion — though its own accountants reportedly warned that the IRS could challenge that classification.Separately, Broadcom was reportedly assembling a $60 billion financing package to help Anthropic and other companies fund their AI chip and infrastructure needs, a deal that could further expand AI capacity nationwide while simultaneously boosting demand for Broadcom's own data-center hardware.Hoffman's upbeat framing stands in contrast to warnings from other prominent voices in and around the industry. AI skeptic Ed Zitron warned last month that the private credit financing fueling the AI data-center boom had become what he called a "brewing crisis," citing rising borrowing costs and mounting construction delays as signs of real financial strain building beneath the surface.Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has also struck a more cautious tone, suggesting the world may need to experience a serious AI-related crisis, such as a major cyberattack or similar catastrophe, before governments and the public take the technology's risks seriously enough to respond with real urgency.
Article Summary: LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman has defended the massive wave of AI infrastructure investment in the United States. He argued that spending on data centers and related projects is providing a significant boost to the broader economy and helping the country to avoid recession. Hoffman emphasized the ripple effects this spending has on local economies, pointing to the range of workers who benefit from data center construction.

Article Title: Meta lets go co-founders and employees of AI startup Virtue AI, four months after the company hired them; Andy Stone admits differences over style of working
Article Text:
Meta lets go co-founders and employees of AI startup Virtue AI, four months after the company hired them; Andy Stone admits differences over style of working

Meta says Virtue AI arrangement did not work out

Meta hired Virtue AI founders in June

Why Meta hired the Virtue AI team

Meta continues AI safety push

Meta has made similar AI team hires

Meta is letting go of employees from an AI security startup it acquired just months ago. The tech giant has reportedly parted ways with Virtue AI co-founders Bo Li, Dawn Song, and Sanmi Koyejo, along with other employees, just four months after bringing them into Meta Superintelligence Labs in June. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone confirmed the departures to Semafor and said the arrangement did not work out as planned because of differences in working styles.The move comes after Meta had recruited the Virtue AI team to strengthen its efforts around AI safety, security and frontier risks. The startup had previously worked with companies including Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as the Commerce Department’s National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST).Meta spokesperson Andy Stone confirmed the departures to Semafor and attributed the decision to differences in how the team worked.“Unfortunately, the arrangement didn’t work out as planned,” Stone said, adding that Meta Superintelligence Labs remains focused on AI safety, alignment and frontier risk.The departures come as Meta continues to shape its AI strategy and expand its capabilities around increasingly advanced AI systems.The company has been investing heavily in artificial intelligence, while AI safety and security have also become a growing focus for technology companies and policymakers.In June, Axios reported that Meta Superintelligence Labs hired Virtue AI co-founders Bo Li, Dawn Song and Sanmi Koyejo, along with other members of the startup’s team.The hiring aimed to strengthen Meta’s security efforts around AI agents at a time when concerns about the safety of increasingly capable AI systems were growing.Virtue AI had developed enterprise AI security tools covering automated red teaming, runtime guardrails and AI governance. The startup had also previously worked with Anthropic, OpenAI and the Commerce Department’s NIST. However, the terms of the arrangement were not disclosed.“As we ship AI products to billions of people and build increasingly capable agents, keeping those systems safe, reliable, and trustworthy is foundational,” the memo says.Li and Song were set to report to Nat Friedman, a Meta Superintelligence Labs executive, while Koyejo was expected to report to Rob Fergus, head of Meta's fundamental AI research lab, FAIR.Meta's decision to bring in the Virtue AI founders reflected the company's broader push to strengthen AI security as it develops more capable models and agents.The startup's work focused on identifying potential risks in AI systems and developing tools to test and safeguard them. Its technology included automated red teaming to identify weaknesses in AI systems, as well as runtime guardrails and governance tools.The hiring also represented another example of Meta bringing in a group of specialised AI researchers and engineers rather than acquiring an entire startup.Despite the departure of the Virtue AI team, Stone said Meta Superintelligence Labs remains focused on AI safety, alignment and frontier risk.The development comes as AI companies face increasing scrutiny over how they develop, test and deploy increasingly capable systems. AI agents, in particular, have become a growing area of focus as companies work on systems that can perform more complex tasks with less human intervention.Meta's decision to recruit the Virtue AI team in June was part of that broader push. However, the arrangement lasted only four months before the company decided to let the employees go.The Virtue AI hiring was also part of Meta's broader strategy to recruit specialised teams from smaller AI companies.Meta poached the founders and team behind Dreamer, an AI startup focused on helping people build agents, in March. The approach allows the company to bring in specialised talent and expertise without necessarily acquiring an entire company.The Virtue AI departures now mark a much shorter-lived version of that strategy, with Meta confirming that differences in working styles contributed to the arrangement ending.The company, however, continues to expand its AI operations as the race to develop increasingly capable models and agents intensifies.
Article Summary: Virtue AI co-founders Bo Li, Dawn Song, and Sanmi Koyejo have been let go by Meta Superintelligence Labs. The tech giant hired the Virtue AI team in June to strengthen its efforts around AI safety, security and frontier risks. The departures come as Meta continues to shape its AI strategy.

Article Title: Days after Sam Altman warned the world that AI is growing too fast and may hurt everyone on the way; he wants world to accept bad things for the benefit of ...
Article Text:
The world should accept some bad things happening, says OpenAI CEO

A pointed contrast with Anthropic

Where the White House stands

A shifting message from Sam Altman

Days after warning that artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly and could cause significant disruption, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that the benefits of the technology justify accepting some risks and argued that AI should remain broadly accessible rather than tightly controlled. "We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency," Altman said in an interview with Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded, according to a Reuters report. Altman said OpenAI and rival AI company Dario Amodei-led Anthropic continue to differ on key questions around AI governance and regulation. "I think there's a lot of daylight," he said, referring to the gap in views between the two companies.In an interview with Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded, Altman laid out his core philosophy plainly, saying the world should accept that some bad things will happen as a trade-off for the benefits of the technology and for giving people real agency over how they use it.He used the interview to draw a sharp line between OpenAI's approach and that of rival Anthropic, acknowledging there's a lot of daylight between the two companies' worldviews on AI regulation.Altman said he understands, even if he disagrees with, the perspective that argues the technology could become so powerful and so dangerous that a single lab in San Francisco should control it entirely, carefully managing how its benefits get distributed to prevent harm. He called that approach a completely unacceptable trade-off, one that runs counter to the lighter-touch regulatory stance OpenAI has consistently backed.Altman was direct about where he draws the line, saying he wouldn't accept a trade-off that guaranteed zero major hacks, zero misuse, and zero scams tied to the technology, because he believes people will ultimately do vastly more good with AI than harm — orders of magnitude more, in his words.Altman's comments land amid a broader, increasingly public rift within the AI industry over how quickly development should proceed and how seriously to weigh the risks posed by increasingly capable systems. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay calling on the industry to "pace the frontier," urging companies to deliberately slow the rate at which they release new capabilities — a position Altman had publicly endorsed at the time, making his latest remarks something of a more nuanced follow-up rather than an outright reversal.The tension within the industry has only intensified since then. An Anthropic researcher resigned in September, stating publicly that the people building AI believe it could kill everyone by the end of the decade. Reuters also reported in September that Anthropic had warned advanced AI models can sometimes behave in ways that run counter to their creators' intentions, including penetrating other companies' systems, attempting to resist shutdown, concealing or manipulating information, or producing outputs that could reasonably be described as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative.Altman's push for a lighter regulatory touch also aligns with the current posture of the Trump administration, which has largely resisted calls for new AI restrictions. President Trump has repeatedly argued that additional rules would put American companies at a competitive disadvantage against Chinese rivals, maintaining that existing law enforcement agencies, including the Justice Department, already provide sufficient safeguards without the need for new AI-specific regulation.Taken together, Altman's latest comments reveal a leader trying to hold two positions at once: publicly acknowledging, as he has in recent weeks, that AI is advancing fast enough to pose genuine risks, while simultaneously resisting the more centralized, tightly controlled approach that figures like Amodei and departing Anthropic researchers argue may be necessary to manage those very risks. For Altman, the calculation remains that broad access and rapid progress, even with their costs, outweigh the alternative of concentrating AI's power and its safeguards in the hands of a few.
Article Summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the benefits of AI justify accepting some risks. He argues that AI should remain broadly accessible rather than tightly controlled. Altman said OpenAI and rival AI company Dario Amodei-led Anthropic continue to differ.

Article Title: California man arrested on charges of smuggling banned Nvidia chips to China; follows arrest of Super Micro Computer founder, may face 20 years in jail
Article Text:
Representative image

California man accused of smuggling Nvidia chips to China

How the alleged scheme worked

FBI warns over advanced AI technology

Lui could face up to 20 years in prison

A California man has been arrested over alleged chip smuggling. The 38-year-old owner of San Gabriel Valley-based Earthmade Computer Inc. is accused of smuggling more than $300 million worth of export-controlled computer servers containing US-manufactured graphics processing units (GPUs) to China. Prosecutors allege that Greg Lui, also known as “Yiu Kong Lui”, used false paperwork and routed the high-end servers through countries including Malaysia and Singapore before they were allegedly re-exported to China.The case follows US authorities' separate arrest of Super Micro Computer co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw in connection with an alleged scheme to divert Nvidia-powered AI servers to China. If convicted of all three charges, Lui could face up to 20 years in prison on the conspiracy and money laundering counts and up to 10 years on the smuggling count.Lui is charged with one count of conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act and Export Administration Regulations, one count of outbound smuggling and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering.“SI is the defining technology of the era,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “The National Security Division will protect the American advantage in the chips that power this technology, a product of our unparalleled innovation and hard work, from illegal diversion by our economic and military adversaries.”According to an indictment returned on Sept. 29, Lui allegedly used Earthmade to buy export-controlled items between 2023 and 2024 and send them to China without required US licences.Prosecutors allege that the equipment was first shipped to Malaysia and Singapore before being re-exported to China. They also allege that Lui provided false documentation to US manufacturers, misrepresenting the intended end users and destinations.From January to October 2024, Earthmade received more than $176 million from two Malaysia-based shipment companies as part of the alleged scheme.In January 2024, Lui allegedly emailed a conspirator about a Malaysian transshipment company seeking 70 servers with export-restricted GPUs.Later that month, he allegedly ordered 27 servers from a US manufacturer for approximately $7.614 million. The servers were shipped from Los Angeles to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, with documents identifying their GPUs as export-controlled equipment that could not be sent to China without a licence.In March 2024, a co-conspirator allegedly told a Malaysian government official that the 27 servers had been transshipped to a China-based buyer.“Protecting America’s national security means keeping our advanced Super Intelligence technology from being used to strengthen our adversaries’ military capabilities,” said First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “This defendant allegedly used false paperwork and shipments through third countries to smuggle more than $300 million in export-controlled computer servers to China. We will aggressively prosecute those who put our national security at risk for profit.”“The FBI’s investigation revealed that Lui allegedly sold the Chinese government hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of American Super Intelligence technology, in clear violation of U.S. export control laws,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “Controlling the export of advanced SI technology is critical to safeguarding our national security and defending the homeland, and the FBI will keep fighting for America’s businesses and economic security. We’re grateful to our partners across the U.S. government and private sector for their assistance, and we’ll continue holding accountable anyone who violates U.S. export laws to enrich themselves and help our adversaries.”“Preventing the illegal export of controlled technology is critical to protecting our national security,” said Special Agent in Charge John E. Helsing of the Department of Defense Office of Inspector General Defense Criminal Investigative Service (DCIS) Western Field Office. “These technologies provide core advantages to U.S. forces, and ensuring they remain safeguarded prevents adversaries from exploiting them. Today’s action underscores our commitment to protecting advanced defense capabilities and enforcing the laws that keep them out of the hands of those who may threaten the United States.”If convicted of all charges, Lui could face a maximum of 20 years in prison on the conspiracy count, 20 years on the money laundering count and 10 years on the smuggling count.The Bureau of Industry and Security, Defense Criminal Investigative Service and FBI are investigating the case. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Colin S. Scott and Joseph S. Guzman, along with Trial Attorney Eli Ross, are prosecuting the case.

Article Title: Apple is making changes to its OS for Macs after users' complain about Meta's AI Agent Muse accessing their 'private data'
Article Text:
Apple's complete statement on updates to Full Disk Access in macOS

Apple is planning to change its Mac operating system, and the reason are AI Agents. The company wants to make it more clear to users when AI agents ask ​to access all of the data on their Macs. The announcement comes after some users have criticized Meta's ‌Muse, an AI agent for accessing their private messages. While on ​Apple's iPhones and iPads, no single app can access data inside another ​app by default, company's Macs are ⁠more flexible. Apple Macs come with a 'Full Disk Access' option that allows apps such as cloud ​backup services to access all the data on a machine, with a user's permission.In an update posted on its developer website, Apple said that some developers were using the Full Disk Access feature in ways that could put users at risk. "Going forward, we will introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely ​wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so ​with very explicit user action," Apple wrote."As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, ‌the ⁠risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy."Apple's announcement comes after a technology ​columnist in Inc magazine accused ​Meta's Muse of ⁠reading private messages on his Mac. "In fact, I remember explicitly choosing not to let it have access to my messages, calendar, and other personal information," he wrote. He claimed that he had not enabled Full Disk Access and further added that when he asked Muse to explain how this occurred, the AI said that it was syncing his "device notifications. " Similarly, a YouTuber named Matt Robb recently said that Muse mishandled a task in which he was selling things on Facebook Marketplace, leading to his address being shared.Meta spokesperson Andy Stone disputed the claims saying that Muse's access to Apple's Messages app ​is strictly ⁠opt-in. "You have to enable both Full Disk Access and the Messages connector for Muse to be able to read your Messages content," Stone wrote on social media platform X, opens new tab. "It ⁠can't read ​your Messages unless you do this. And it ​can be revoked at any time.""We give developers powerful APIs to build incredible capabilities into their apps for Apple products, backed by a set of controls designed to protect users’ private data. Full Disk Access largely sidesteps these controls in order to allow backup apps to function properly on the Mac. Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy. "
